title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Big Question
What can an analysis claim when some linguistic measurements were never observed?

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Data
A vowel study records duration, F1, and F3.
The F3 tracker fails for some tokens.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Challenge
A blank cell is not a measured value. Deleting or filling it can change the quantity being estimated.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Possibility
Imputation replaces a missing value with one or more estimates from a model or rule.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-historic.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
This Module

Represent where measurements are absent.
State how absence may depend on observed and unseen values.
Determine what deletion estimates.
Reconstruct missing cells and validate the procedure.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Missingness patterns
Representing blank cells

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Question
Where are duration, F1, and F3 absent in the acoustic table?

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
A missingness indicator records whether a potential measurement was observed.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Method
\[
R_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1&\text{if }Y_{ij}\text{ is observed},\\
0&\text{if }Y_{ij}\text{ is missing}.
\end{cases}
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Data
\[
\mathbf R=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&1\\
1&1&0\\
1&1&1\\
1&0&0\\
1&1&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Output
Column counts locate measurements with loss.
Row counts locate tokens with little information.
Pattern counts locate measurements that disappear together.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Challenge
An association between vowel and missing F3 does not identify the process that caused the association.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Upshot
The missingness pattern is observed. Its generating mechanism is not.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Missingness mechanisms
Dependence on observed and unseen measurements

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
A missingness mechanism states how observation depends on measured and missing values.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Method
The object of interest is
\[
P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}}).
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Values are missing completely at random (MCAR) when observation depends on neither observed nor missing measurements.
\[
P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}})=P(R=1)
\]

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Values are missing at random (MAR) when observation may depend on observed measurements but not additionally on the missing value.
\[
P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}},Y_{\mathrm{mis}})=P(R=1\mid Y_{\mathrm{obs}})
\]

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Values are missing not at random (MNAR) when observation still depends on the unseen value after observed measurements are considered.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Data
All three simple sentence trials are observed.
Only one of three complex sentence trials is observed.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Interpretation
The pattern is compatible with MAR through observed complexity and with MNAR through unseen reading time.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Challenge
A plot cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR because it cannot display the unseen values.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Upshot
State a mechanism at the participant, session, or trial level where absence occurs.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Complete case analysis
What deletion estimates

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Data
F3 is absent for the three longest of eight fricative tokens.
A software function silently drops those rows.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Complete case analysis, also called listwise deletion, retains rows observed on every required variable.

[Sources]
https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/sec-MCAR.html

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Method
For required variables \(J\),
\[
C_i=\prod_{j\in J}R_{ij}.
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Result #1
Mean duration over all eight tokens is 135 milliseconds.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Result #2
Mean duration among the five complete tokens is 120 milliseconds.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Interpretation
The complete case mean describes tokens with observed duration and F3.
It does not describe all eight tokens.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Surprising Fact
If five required variables are independently observed in ninety percent of rows,
\[
P(C_i=1)=.9^5\approx.59.
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Upshot
Deletion can lose far more rows than any one column suggests and can change the target population.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Iterative PCA imputation
Reconstructing missing cells

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Question
Can correlated acoustic measurements help reconstruct an absent measurement?

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer
Iterative PCA imputation repeatedly updates missing cells with a low rank reconstruction while fixing observed cells.

[Sources]
https://cran.r-project.org/package=missMDA

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Method
Initialize missing cells. Fit a rank \(K\) reconstruction. Replace only missing cells. Restore observed measurements. Repeat until the updates stabilize.
Recall centering and scaling and reconstruction.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Data
\[
\mathbf Y=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&-1\\
0&?\\
1&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Output
Column mean initialization fills the missing cell with zero.
The rank one reconstruction returns the same matrix.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Important Point #1
The component count controls which relations inform the reconstruction.
It must be selected without access to the masked values.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Important Point #2
An imputed cell is a prediction under a low rank assumption. It is not an observed measurement.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Challenge
PCA imputation may pull rare vowels, nonlinear relations, or extreme values toward the dominant linear structure.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Validating imputation
Masking values that are known

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Question
How can we evaluate reconstruction when the naturally missing values are unknown?

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Approach
Hide measured values on purpose, fit without them, and compare their reconstructions with the held aside measurements.
This is the training and test separation applied to matrix cells.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Method
For masked cells \(M\),
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(M)=\frac{1}{|M|}\sum_{(i,j)\in M}
(y_{ij}-\widehat y_{ij}^{(-M)})^2.
\]

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Data
Mask a measured value of \(2.9\).
The column mean from the remaining values is \(2.5\).

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Output
\[
(2.9-2.5)^2=.16
\]
The masked value was unavailable during fitting.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Challenge
Uniform masks may test common vowels and central values even when natural failures concern rare vowels or extremes.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Important Point #1
Estimate centering, scaling, component directions, and tuning choices after masking.
Otherwise information from the masked value leaks into its prediction.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Important Point #2
Retain errors by vowel, speaker group, language, and measurement column before averaging.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Upshot
Poor reconstruction falsifies an imputation procedure under the tested mask. Low error does not reveal the naturally missing values.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Conclusion
Observed values, missing values, and predictions

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Big Question
What can an analysis claim when some linguistic measurements were never observed?

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Answer

Encode where measurements are absent.
Separate visible patterns from assumptions about the missingness mechanism.
State which rows a deletion analysis targets.
Preserve the distinction between observed and imputed cells.
Validate the complete reconstruction procedure under realistic masks.

title: Reasoning about missing linguistic measurements
text:
Upshot
No completion procedure establishes its own assumptions. The report must state what was observed, assumed, reconstructed, and still unknown.

Data
A unit of analysis may be a speaker represented by language-use ratings, a vowel token represented by F1 and F2, or a language represented by grammatical features.

text:
Challenge
The rows, features, scaling, distance, and candidate number of groups all help determine the structure that can be found.

Finding unobserved groups
Two statistical representations

\mathbf X=
\begin{bmatrix}
5&1\\
4&2\\
1&5

\]

Method
Each row is one speaker. The two columns define similarity. Identifiers and variables reserved for interpretation remain outside the feature matrix.

Defining the geometry

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Answer
Euclidean distance combines squared column differences.
\[
d(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_j)=
\sqrt{\sum_m(x_{im}-x_{jm})^2}
\]

Penn State STAT 505


[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Challenge
A difference of 1,000 tokens dominates a difference of one rating point before scaling. Changing token units can therefore change the learned geometry.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Approach
Standardization expresses each difference in observed standard-deviation units. During validation, estimate means and standard deviations from training rows only.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Upshot
Equal observed variance does not imply equal reliability or theoretical importance. Euclidean distance remains a linguistic assumption about comparable differences.

K-means clustering
Alternating assignments and centroid updates

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Method
K-means clustering minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances.
\[
W=\sum_i\lVert\mathbf x_i-\boldsymbol\mu_{z_i}\rVert^2
\]

Penn State STAT 505


[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Implementation

Assign every row to its nearest centroid.
Replace each centroid with the mean of its assigned rows.
Repeat until assignments no longer change.

Question
For points \((0,0)\) and \((0,2)\) in one cluster, why is the updated centroid \((0,1)\)?

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data

K-means can converge to a local minimum. Compare the fitted loss over several initializations.

Within-cluster loss
Comparing candidate values of K

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Surprising Fact
Training within-cluster loss cannot increase when another centroid is added. More centroids can reproduce the earlier solution and may improve it.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Method
An elbow plot displays fitted within-cluster loss against \(K\). The elbow method looks for diminishing reductions.

Penn State STAT 505


[Sources]

https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat505/Lesson14

Upshot
An elbow may be ambiguous and depends on representation, scaling, distance, and initialization. Training compactness does not establish held-out performance.

Silhouette widths
Cohesion relative to separation

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Answer
A silhouette width compares average within-cluster distance \(a(i)\) with distance to the nearest alternative cluster \(b(i)\).

R cluster reference


[Sources]

https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/cluster/html/silhouette.html

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Method
\[
s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max\{a(i),b(i)\}}.
\]
Positive values favor the assigned cluster. Negative values favor a neighboring cluster.

Silhouette widths diagnose compact separation under the chosen distance. They do not establish that the groups are linguistic categories.

Question
Without observed group labels, what can a clustering predict for a row omitted during fitting?

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Answer
Assign the held-out row to its nearest training centroid and record its squared distance to that centroid as predictive loss.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Implementation

Estimate scaling from training rows.
Fit candidate centroids to those rows.
Transform held-out rows with training scaling.
Compare paired nearest-centroid losses.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data

Upshot
Lower loss establishes better numerical prediction under the declared geometry. It does not establish recovery of an unobserved linguistic category.

Overlapping component distributions

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Data
Peterson and Barney measured F1 and F2 for vowel tokens in an /hVd/ frame. Intended vowel labels remain outside the mixture fit.

Peterson and Barney 1952; phonTools pb52


[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875
https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Method
A Gaussian mixture model (GMM) combines weighted Gaussian component densities.
\[
p(\mathbf x_i)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i;\boldsymbol\mu_k,\boldsymbol\Sigma_k)
\]

scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models


[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Interpretation
Each covariance matrix controls component spread and orientation. Every component contributes density to every token.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Challenge
A covariance can collapse around very few observations and produce an unbounded likelihood. A tiny fitted component may therefore be a numerical failure.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Upshot
A component is a distributional summary under the chosen representation. It is not automatically a phoneme or intended vowel category.
Return to the notes

Normalizing component contributions

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Answer
The posterior probability of component membership applies Bayes’ rule:
\[
\Pr(Z_i=k\mid\mathbf x_i)=
\frac{\pi_kp(\mathbf x_i\mid Z_i=k)}{\sum_h\pi_hp(\mathbf x_i\mid Z_i=h)}.
\]

scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models


[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Interpretation
These probabilities, often called responsibilities, sum to one for each token. A hard assignment discards the remaining membership uncertainty.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Upshot
Label switching means that component numbers have no stable linguistic identity across separate fits.

Method
The expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm alternates conditional expectations of component labels with parameter updates.

scikit-learn, Gaussian mixture models


[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/mixture.html

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data

Compute responsibilities under provisional parameters.
Update weights, means, and covariances with responsibility-weighted quantities.
Repeat until the fitted objective stabilizes.

Method
For a held-out token, use log loss
\[
L_i(M)=-\log p_M(\mathbf x_i\mid D_{\mathrm{train}}).
\]
Lower loss means higher fitted predictive density.

title: Finding unobserved groups in linguistic data
text:
Implementation

Hold out every token from each test speaker.
Estimate scaling and the complete mixture inside training data.
Return token losses to held-out speakers.
Examine stability across starts and speaker splits.

Held-out speaker loss evaluates density for absent speakers under the stated normalization information. It remains conditional on the candidate set and representation.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
text:
Suppose we count every represented word token in a corpus. Some word types occur many times, while most occur rarely. We would like to describe this imbalance without yet claiming to explain it.
Begin by sorting the word types from highest frequency to lowest frequency. The most frequent type receives rank 1, the next receives rank 2, and so on.
The table has two numerical columns, but they do not come from independent measurements. Frequency is the token count for a type. Rank is assigned after the types have been ordered by that count.
The frequency falls roughly as rank rises. The type at rank 2 occurs about half as often as the type at rank 1. The type at rank 3 occurs about one third as often.
This inverse relation is the basic form of Zipf’s law:
f(r)\propto\frac{1}{r^\alpha}.
Here r is a word type’s rank, f(r) is its frequency, and \alpha controls how quickly frequency falls as rank rises. A value near one gives the familiar inverse rank pattern.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
text:
First decide what was counted
Even this small table requires representational choices.

What counts as a token? Punctuation marks might be included or removed.
What counts as the same type? run and runs might be separate forms or members of one lemma.
What counts as the corpus? One novel, a collection of conversations, and a balanced genre sample represent different populations of tokens.
How are ties in frequency ranked?

Changing these choices changes both the frequencies and the ranks. Zipf’s law is a pattern in a represented dataset. It is not recovered before tokenization and type definition.
Consider lemmatization. If run, runs, ran, and running are grouped under one lemma, their counts are added. The lemma may move to a higher rank than any individual form occupied. Other types may then move to lower ranks even though their own token counts did not change.
This dependence of rank on the full table should remain visible in the analysis statement.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
section: Work through the inverse pattern by hand
text:
Work through the inverse pattern by hand
For the simplest case, set \alpha=1. We can write the proportional relation as

f(r)=\frac{C}{r},

where C is a constant. If the rank 1 type has frequency 10,000, then

C=f(1)\times1=10{,}000.

The simple curve predicts

\begin{aligned}
f(2)&=10{,}000/2=5{,}000,\\
f(3)&=10{,}000/3\approx3{,}333,\\
f(4)&=10{,}000/4=2{,}500.
\end{aligned}

Compare those predictions with the observed counts.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
section: Reproduce the calculation in base R
text:
Reproduce the calculation in base R


Code
word <- c("the", "of", "and", "to")
frequency <- c(10000, 5100, 3400, 2450)
rank <- seq_along(frequency)

zipf_prediction <- frequency[1] / rank

data.frame(
  word = word,
  frequency = frequency,
  rank = rank,
  prediction = zipf_prediction,
  difference = frequency - zipf_prediction
)


The code makes one fixed comparison. It uses the rank 1 count to set C and then checks the other ranks. It does not estimate \alpha, select among mechanisms, or establish that the corpus follows an exact law.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
text:
Inspect the broad pattern
Piantadosi plots frequency against rank for a large corpus.

The broad inverse relation is striking. The second plot shows, however, that the data do not lie exactly on one ideal curve. The deviations are systematic, especially among very frequent and very infrequent types.

We should thus keep two questions separate.

Does an inverse rank frequency curve describe the broad pattern?
What process produced the particular frequencies and deviations in this corpus?

The first question is descriptive. The second asks for an explanation.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
section: Why curve matching does not identify a mechanism
text:
Why curve matching does not identify a mechanism
Many proposed mechanisms can produce an approximately Zipfian pattern. They make different claims about memory, lexical organization, communication, and textual growth. If incompatible mechanisms produce the same broad curve, then matching that curve cannot distinguish among them.
A useful account must make additional predictions. It might predict which meanings receive frequent forms, how the curve changes in a restricted genre, how local frequencies change through a text, or where syntactic categories depart from the overall pattern.
Reproducing a broad curve does not explain its source. The fit may be real while the mechanistic conclusion remains unsupported. The relevant criticism is not that the curve is imperfect. It is that the curve alone does not separate the proposed account from alternatives.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
text:
State the narrow target
For this rank frequency analysis, we can write:

One observation represents one word type in the chosen corpus. Its response is the number of represented tokens assigned to that type. Rank is assigned after sorting those counts. The target is the relation between rank and frequency under this tokenization, type definition, and corpus sample.

This statement does not claim that the fitted curve explains lexical choice, memory, or communication. Those broader claims require comparisons that differ across the competing accounts.

title: A first pattern: Zipf’s law
text:
Check your understanding

If the rank 1 frequency is 12,000 and \alpha=1, compute the simple predicted frequencies at ranks 2, 3, and 4.
Suppose two forms are combined under one lemma. Explain why the ranks of types outside that lemma may change even if their counts do not.
What does a small observed minus predicted value establish? What does it not establish about the source of the pattern?
Give one additional prediction that could distinguish two mechanisms that both produce an inverse rank frequency curve.

We now have a linguistic pattern and a precise statement of what its rows represent. The next pages build the probability objects needed to describe such patterns, beginning with sample spaces.

title: The product rule
text:
Suppose a corpus annotation tells us two things that are easy to summarize separately: half of the represented pronouns are plural, and among plural pronouns, eighty percent are accusative. How can we recover the probability that a pronoun is both plural and accusative?
The definition of conditional probability already contains the answer:
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)}{\mathbb{P}(P)}.
Here P is the plural event and A is the accusative event. Multiply both sides by \mathbb{P}(P):
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)
=\mathbb{P}(A\cap P).
Writing the joint probability first gives
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
=\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P).
This expression is the product rule, also called the multiplication rule. It writes one joint probability as a product of a conditional probability and the probability of its condition.

title: The product rule
section: Reconstruct the joint probability by hand
text:
Reconstruct the joint probability by hand
The pronoun measure gives

\mathbb{P}(P)=.50

and

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.

Substitute these two values into the product rule:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
&=\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)\\
&=.80\times.50\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}

The multiplication has a direct interpretation. The conditioning event P receives half of the total mass. The event A receives eighty percent of that plural mass. Eighty percent of one half is .40.
We can check the same logic with counts. Imagine 100 pronoun tokens.

If 50 are plural, then the plural event contains 50 tokens.
If 80 percent of those 50 are accusative, then 40 tokens are both plural and accusative.
Those 40 tokens make up 40 percent of all 100 tokens.

The product rule is the proportional version of this count calculation.


Code
p_plural <- .50
p_acc_given_plural <- .80

p_plural_and_acc <- p_acc_given_plural * p_plural
p_plural_and_acc


The result is .4.

title: The product rule
section: Reverse the order of the factors
text:
Reverse the order of the factors
An intersection is symmetric:

A\cap P=P\cap A.

We can thus begin from the opposite conditional probability:

\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)
=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A).

In the toy measure,

\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)=\frac{.40}{.70}

and \mathbb{P}(A)=.70. The reversed product is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)
&=\frac{.40}{.70}\times.70\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}

The factors differ across the two orders. The product does not. Both products reconstruct the mass in the same intersection.
This gives the identity

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\mathbb{P}(P)
=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A).

We will use exactly this equality on the next page. No additional probability assumption has been made.

title: The product rule
section: What the product rule does and does not claim
text:
What the product rule does and does not claim
The product rule is an algebraic rewriting of a joint probability. It does not claim that A and P are unrelated. In fact, the factor \mathbb{P}(A\mid P) explicitly allows the probability of A to depend on the condition P.
This point matters in linguistic applications. If a speaker’s use of a reduced form depends on whether the word is predictable in context, we can still factor the joint event as

\mathbb{P}(\text{reduced}\cap\text{predictable})
=\mathbb{P}(\text{reduced}\mid\text{predictable})
\mathbb{P}(\text{predictable}).

The product rule represents the dependence through the conditional term.

title: The product rule
section: A product does not imply independence
text:
A product does not imply independence
A product representation does not by itself imply independence. The presence of a multiplication sign does not justify replacing

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)

with

\mathbb{P}(A).

That replacement is a separate claim about independence, which has not yet been established. The product rule itself holds whenever the conditional probability is defined.

title: The product rule
text:
Check your understanding

Starting from the definition of \mathbb{P}(P\mid A), derive \mathbb{P}(A\cap P)=\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A).
Suppose \mathbb{P}(P)=.30 and \mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.60. Compute \mathbb{P}(A\cap P) and interpret the result among 100 tokens.
Explain why the two orders of the product rule have different factors but the same product.
Which unjustified substitution treats the two chain rule factors as independent?

The two orders reconstruct the same intersection. On the next page, we equate those products and solve for a reversed conditional probability.

title: Sample spaces
text:
Suppose that we want to describe the form of one English personal pronoun token. We may eventually want to ask whether the form is nominative, accusative, singular, or plural. Before we can ask any of those questions, however, we need to decide what one possible result of the observation looks like.
This is a representation problem. A recording may contain them, a transcript may contain the spelling them, and an annotation may contain the label third person plural accusative. Each record describes the same token at a different level. A probability model must commit to one of those levels.
We will begin with the surface form. One possible list is
\Omega
=\{\textit{I},\textit{me},\textit{you},\textit{he},\textit{him},
\textit{she},\textit{her},\textit{we},\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
The symbol \Omega denotes the sample space. Each member of \Omega is an outcome. If the recorded form is her, the realized outcome is one member of the sample space.
We can now state the definition.
The word represented matters. This sample space does not claim that English has exactly eleven pronouns. It omits reflexive forms, possessive forms, and dialectal variants. Those omissions might be harmless for a study of nominative and accusative personal pronouns. They would make the space unusable for a study of reflexive choice.

title: Sample spaces
text:
Check the representation by hand
At this stage, we have not assigned probabilities. We can only ask whether a proposed outcome belongs to the sample space. The notation x\in\Omega says that x is a member of \Omega, while x\notin\Omega says that it is not.
For the space above,

\textit{him}\in\Omega
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\textit{herself}\notin\Omega.

Work through what these statements mean. The first says that the model has a possible result corresponding to him. The second says that the model has no possible result corresponding to herself. It does not say that speakers cannot produce herself.
A minimal base R representation makes the same membership check.


Code
omega <- c("I", "me", "you", "he", "him", "she", "her",
           "we", "us", "they", "them")

"him" %in% omega
"herself" %in% omega


The first expression returns TRUE; the second returns FALSE. The code is only a finite encoding of the set written above. It does not yet define which outcomes are common.

title: Sample spaces
text:
Granularity changes the outcome
Now consider a vowel production study. At least three sample spaces are possible.

One outcome is an entire recording.
One outcome is a segmented vowel token.
One outcome is an acoustic measurement taken at a specified point in a vowel.

These spaces do not give three interchangeable descriptions of one observation. They answer the question “what could happen once?” differently.
Suppose a speaker produces heed twice and we measure F1 at the vowel midpoint. Under the second representation, the two vowel tokens are two possible observed units. Under the third representation, values such as 285 Hz and 301 Hz are possible observed results. A question about whether the vowel was /i/ belongs naturally to the token representation. A question about whether F1 was below 300 Hz belongs naturally to the measurement representation.
This choice also determines what must accompany the observed value. In a judgment experiment, the response value 6 alone may not identify the outcome that matters for analysis. We may instead represent an outcome as the pair

\langle\text{participant and sentence trial},\ 6\rangle.

The sample space should contain the distinctions needed by the linguistic question.

title: Sample spaces
section: A common failure: treating omission as impossibility
text:
A common failure: treating omission as impossibility
An omitted outcome is not an impossible result. A space may appear complete because every listed outcome is assigned a place, even though the list omits results that the observation process can produce.
For instance, a forced choice experiment may offer the responses agent and patient. If participants can also skip the trial, then

\Omega=\{\text{agent},\text{patient}\}

does not represent the recorded process unless skipped trials are removed by an explicit rule. A model using this space cannot distinguish a skipped response from missing data created later in processing.
The repair is not to add every conceivable linguistic object. It is to state the observation process and include every result that process can deliver for the question at hand.

title: Sample spaces
text:
Check your understanding

A study records a seven point judgment for each participant and sentence. Give one sample space whose outcomes are response values. Then give a different sample space whose outcomes retain trial identity.
In the pronoun space above, what does \textit{herself}\notin\Omega claim about the model? What does it not claim about English?
A corpus annotation distinguishes nouns, verbs, and adjectives but labels every other token OTHER. Is OTHER an outcome? Explain your answer from the stored annotation process.
A vowel study stores one F1 trajectory with eleven time points for each token. What question would make one trajectory a suitable outcome? What different question would make one time point a suitable outcome?

Once we know what can happen once, we can group outcomes that give the same answer to a linguistic question. The next page introduces those groups as events.

title: Turning linguistic records into data
text:
Suppose we have made a recording of a speaker producing the word heed. What is the observation in this recording?
There is no single answer. We might represent the recording as one waveform, as one word token, as one vowel token, or as a sequence of acoustic measurements taken through the vowel. The recording contains information that supports each representation. It does not choose among them.
This is the first decision in a statistical analysis: what does one observation represent? The entity represented by one observation is the unit of analysis.

title: Turning linguistic records into data
text:
Begin with the stored record
A record is a stored artifact. Recordings, corpus documents, response logs, and annotation files are all records.
One record may contain many possible observations. A ten-minute interview is one audio file, but it may contain hundreds of word tokens and dozens of vowel tokens. Conversely, several records may contribute information about one observation. If we summarize a speaker across three recording sessions, the speaker-level observation draws on three files.
File count thus tells us how the material is stored. It does not tell us how many observations the analysis contains.

\langle\text{participant},\text{sentence},\text{region}\rangle.

We can check this claim directly. p01 does not identify a row because that participant appears repeatedly. (p01, s17) still does not identify a row because the sentence has several regions. Adding the region makes the identifier unique in this design.

Watch what aggregation changes
Suppose we sum the regional reading times within each participant and sentence. The new table has one row per participant and sentence, so the region column is no longer part of the key.
Suppose we then average across participants. The new table has one row per sentence. The participant column is no longer part of the key either.

Aggregation is not always wrong. It is a transformation with consequences. We need to determine what information the transformation discards.

title: Turning linguistic records into data
text:
Tokens and types
Linguists often switch between tokens and types. A token is an occurrence in a particular context. A type groups occurrences that the analysis treats as equivalent.
Consider ten occurrences of runs. They are ten orthographic word tokens. They belong to one word-form type, runs. A lemmatized analysis may group them with occurrences of run, ran, and running under the lemma run.
There is nothing automatic about the grouping. A study of inflection must distinguish run from runs. A study of lemma frequency may deliberately collapse them.
The choice changes the unit:







question
useful unit




Does discourse context affect the choice of a dative construction?
one construction token


Do verbs differ in their preference for the dative construction?
one verb type, perhaps summarized across tokens


Does one speaker change construction use over an interview?
one speaker by time segment observation



The first analysis preserves contextual variation among tokens. The second emphasizes lexical variation among types. Neither representation is generally better. They support different comparisons.

title: Turning linguistic records into data
text:
Repetition remains repetition
A rectangular table does not claim that its rows are independent. In the reading-time table, participant p01 occurs in several rows and sentence s17 occurs in several rows. Those repetitions remain present even if every row has a unique observation key.
This distinction is easy to miss:

a unique key tells us that two rows are not the same observation;
repeated identifiers tell us that two observations share a participant, item, speaker, word, language, or another source of variation.

Later models can represent these shared sources. At this stage, the important step is to retain the identifiers in the table.

title: Turning linguistic records into data
text:
Keep three levels separate
Three questions help diagnose a proposed dataset.
First, where was the response measured? A judgment might be recorded on every participant and sentence trial.
Second, what does one response in the analysis represent? We might retain each trial or average the judgments by sentence.
Third, what should the claim generalize to? We might want a statement about the tested sentences, new sentences of the same constructions, the tested participants, or a broader population of speakers.
These answers need not be identical. A trial-level analysis may support generalization to new participants and new items when the design contains replication across both. But many tokens from one speaker do not supply replication across speakers. More rows at one level do not create information at another level.

title: Turning linguistic records into data
section: Write the unit before analyzing the response
text:
Write the unit before analyzing the response
Before plotting or modeling, complete this sentence:

One observation represents ______.

Then ask:

Which columns uniquely identify that observation?
Which speakers, items, words, languages, documents, or sites repeat?
Which variation has already been removed by preprocessing or averaging?
Does the dataset contain replication at the level of the intended claim?

For a corpus of dative tokens, a useful answer might be:

One observation represents one attested dative construction token. The observation key combines the document and token position. Speakers, verbs, and documents repeat across observations. The analysis retains both lexical and discourse-context variation.

This statement does not yet choose a probability distribution or regression model. It tells us what those later models must represent.

title: Turning linguistic records into data
text:
Test the distinction

A corpus contains 50,000 word tokens from 20 interviews with five speakers. Give an observation key for a token analysis. Then describe a speaker-level table and state which variation the aggregation removes.
An acceptability experiment presents 40 sentences to each of 100 participants. What does one row represent if the table contains one judgment per row? Which identifiers must be retained?
A typological database contains two inventories for the same language from different sources. Is language a sufficient observation key? What additional identifier is needed?

The next page begins with a research question and works toward a comparison that the observations can express.

title: From linguistic records to probabilities
text:
A statistical analysis does not begin when we fit a model. It begins when we decide what one observation is.
An audio file might become a table with one row per speaker, one row per word, one row per vowel token, or several rows per vowel token. A corpus might become a table of documents, sentences, tokens, or lexical types. Each choice preserves some distinctions and removes others. A later model can only describe the distinctions that the dataset retains.
This module develops that point in two stages. The first stage concerns linguistic records and numerical patterns. The second builds a probability model one object at a time.

title: From linguistic records to probabilities
text:
From records to comparisons
We begin with turning linguistic records into data. That page separates a stored record from the unit represented by one row. It also asks which identifiers repeat and which variation disappears during aggregation.
The next page turns a research question into a comparison. It specifies the response, the linguistic predictor, the observations being compared, and the estimand. These decisions state what a later numerical result is supposed to mean.
Zipf’s law supplies the first worked linguistic pattern. The rank and frequency calculation is simple enough to do by hand, but its interpretation is not. The example separates describing a curve from explaining why that curve appears.

title: From linguistic records to probabilities
section: From possibilities to a probability model
text:
From possibilities to a probability model
The probability sequence has a strict order.

A sample space lists the possible outcomes under a declared representation.
An event groups outcomes that answer a linguistic question in the same way.
A sigma-algebra states which of those groups the model can measure.
A generated sigma-algebra is the smallest sigma-algebra forced by a chosen set of distinctions.
A probability measure assigns coherent numerical mass to the measurable events.
Mutual exclusivity states when two events cannot occur together.
Joint probability measures the event in which two properties occur together.
Conditional probability rescales probability within a stated event.
The product rule reconstructs a joint probability from a conditional probability and its condition.
Bayes’ rule reverses the direction of a conditional probability while retaining event prevalence.
Independence states when conditioning on one event does not change the probability of another.

Each page uses only objects introduced earlier in this list. The sequence stops after independence so that later numerical objects can be introduced in their own module.

title: From linguistic records to probabilities
section: A question to carry through the module
text:
A question to carry through the module
For any linguistic dataset, keep asking the same question:

Which represented outcomes and distinctions make this probability statement meaningful?

If the answer is not available, the numerical calculation may still be correct while the linguistic interpretation remains unsupported. The purpose of the foundations sequence is to make that representation visible before adding more elaborate models.
The chapter dependency graph places this chapter within the full course. Begin with turning linguistic records into data.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
text:
Suppose that a linguistic analysis is concerned with two distinctions: whether a pronoun is plural and whether it is accusative. We want a sigma-algebra that measures both distinctions and every event forced by combining them. We do not want to add unrelated distinctions by hand.
The preceding page introduced a sigma-algebra as a collection of measurable events. If P is the plural event and A is the accusative event, then
\sigma(P,A)
denotes the smallest sigma-algebra containing both P and A. The collection \{P,A\} is a generating set, and \sigma(P,A) is the sigma-algebra generated by that set.
The word smallest does the work. Any sigma-algebra containing P and A must also contain their complements, intersections, and countable unions. The generated sigma-algebra contains those forced events but no additional distinctions.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
section: Begin from a finite pronoun space
text:
Begin from a finite pronoun space
Use the four outcome sample space

\Omega_4
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.

Define the generators

P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}

and

A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}.

The two distinctions cross. A form may be plural or singular, and it may be accusative or nominative.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
text:
Find the atoms by hand
For a finite space, intersect each generator or its complement. The nonempty intersections are

\begin{aligned}
P\cap A &= \{\textit{them}\},\\
P\cap A^c &= \{\textit{they}\},\\
P^c\cap A &= \{\textit{him}\},\\
P^c\cap A^c &= \{\textit{he}\}.
\end{aligned}

These four sets are the atoms produced by the generators. They do not overlap, and every outcome belongs to exactly one of them.
Why begin with atoms? Any event constructed from P, A, and the set operations must treat every outcome inside an atom alike. The generators provide no operation that can separate two outcomes once they share all generator memberships.
In this small example, each atom contains one outcome. Every subset of \Omega_4 can thus be written as a union of atoms. It follows that

\sigma(P,A)=2^{\Omega_4}.

Since there are four atoms, there are 2^4=16 unions of atoms, including the empty union \varnothing and the union of all four atoms \Omega_4.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
section: Inspect the construction in base R
text:
Inspect the construction in base R
The finite set operations can be reproduced directly.


Code
omega <- c("he", "him", "they", "them")
plural <- c("they", "them")
accusative <- c("him", "them")

plural_acc <- intersect(plural, accusative)
plural_nom <- intersect(plural, setdiff(omega, accusative))
singular_acc <- intersect(setdiff(omega, plural), accusative)
singular_nom <- intersect(setdiff(omega, plural),
                          setdiff(omega, accusative))

list(plural_acc, plural_nom, singular_acc, singular_nom)


The output contains the four singleton atoms. The code mirrors the hand calculation, so it is useful as a check rather than as a substitute for identifying the intersections.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
section: See what a coarser generator leaves hidden
text:
See what a coarser generator leaves hidden
Now generate a sigma-algebra from P alone. Its two atoms are

P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}

and

P^c=\{\textit{he},\textit{him}\}.

Every event in \sigma(P) is a union of these two atoms. The generated sigma-algebra is thus

\sigma(P)=\{\varnothing,P,P^c,\Omega_4\}.

This space cannot distinguish they from them. Both outcomes have the same membership in the only generator. Adding A splits each number atom by case, producing the four smaller atoms above.
Generation thus makes a representational decision explicit. The generators state which linguistic distinctions the model can recover.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
section: When the generators omit a needed distinction
text:
When the generators omit a needed distinction
Outcomes that share every generator membership cannot be compared within the generated sigma-algebra. Suppose a model uses only P to generate its sigma-algebra but later asks whether plural pronouns are nominative or accusative. The outcomes they and them occupy the same atom, so the generated sigma-algebra contains no event that separates them.
Adding more observations does not repair a sigma-algebra that lacks the needed distinction. The missing distinction concerns the representation, not the sample size. We must add a case generator before asking the case question.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
text:
A finite construction procedure
For the finite spaces used here, the procedure is mechanical.

List every intersection formed by choosing each generator or its complement.
Remove intersections that are empty.
Treat the remaining intersections as atoms.
Form every union of those atoms.

The resulting collection is the smallest sigma-algebra containing the generators.

title: Generating a sigma-algebra
text:
Check your understanding

Starting from P alone, list its atoms and all four events in \sigma(P).
Explain why adding A separates they from them.
Suppose a third generator T marks third person, but every outcome in \Omega_4 is third person. Does T split any atom? Why not?
If three generators produce six nonempty atoms, how many unions of atoms belong to the generated sigma-algebra?

Generation tells us which events the model can distinguish. It does not say how likely any event is. The next page adds that numerical assignment.

title: Sigma-algebras
text:
Suppose that our pronoun model can measure whether a form is plural. It would be incoherent for the same model to lack a measurable event for “not plural.” The second question is the complement of the first, so the model must keep the two questions together.
This requirement motivates a sigma-algebra, also called an event space. A sigma-algebra is the collection of events to which a probability model can assign probabilities. We write this collection as \mathcal{F}.
To see why the collection needs structure, use the four outcome sample space
\Omega_4
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
Let P be the plural event:
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
Its complement is
P^c=\{\textit{he},\textit{him}\}.
If plural number is the only distinction that the model measures, one possible sigma-algebra is
\mathcal{F}_P
=\{\varnothing,P,P^c,\Omega_4\}.
This collection lets us ask whether a pronoun is plural or singular. It does not let us ask whether the pronoun is accusative, because the accusative event is not in \mathcal{F}_P.

title: Sigma-algebras
section: Check closure one requirement at a time
text:
Check closure one requirement at a time
A sigma-algebra must remain coherent when we negate or combine measurable questions. It satisfies three requirements.

The complete sample space \Omega belongs to \mathcal{F}.
If B belongs to \mathcal{F}, then its complement B^c also belongs to \mathcal{F}.
If B_1,B_2,\ldots belong to \mathcal{F}, then their union \bigcup_i B_i also belongs to \mathcal{F}.

The first requirement ensures that the certain event is measurable. The second ensures that negating a measurable question gives another measurable question. The third ensures that combining measurable alternatives gives another measurable question.
These requirements also supply events that were not listed directly. Since \Omega\in\mathcal{F}, closure under complements gives

\Omega^c=\varnothing\in\mathcal{F}.

Intersections follow from complements and unions. De Morgan’s law gives

B\cap C=(B^c\cup C^c)^c.

Thus a sigma-algebra that is closed under complements and countable unions is also closed under intersections.

title: Sigma-algebras
text:
Work through a failed collection
Consider the proposed collection

\mathcal{G}=\{\Omega_4,P\}.

We can test it by hand.

It contains \Omega_4, so it passes the first requirement.
It contains P but not P^c, so it fails the second requirement.
It also lacks \varnothing, which must appear as \Omega_4^c.

Adding P^c and \varnothing repairs these failures and produces \mathcal{F}_P.
We can encode the four events in base R. The code does not establish the general mathematical definition, but it lets us inspect this finite case.


Code
omega <- c("he", "him", "they", "them")
plural <- c("they", "them")
singular <- setdiff(omega, plural)

event_space <- list(
  impossible = character(0),
  plural = plural,
  singular = singular,
  certain = omega
)

event_space


Notice what the list omits. The singleton event \{\textit{them}\} is a subset of \Omega_4, but it is not an event in \mathcal{F}_P. The model represents them as an outcome while declining to measure a question that isolates it.

title: Sigma-algebras
text:
What the sigma-algebra means
The sample space and sigma-algebra answer different representation questions.

\Omega states which individual outcomes exist in the model.
\mathcal{F} states which groupings of those outcomes can receive probabilities.

For a small finite sample space, we will often use the power set 2^\Omega, the collection containing every subset of \Omega. In that case, every possible grouping of the represented outcomes is measurable. The smaller sigma-algebra \mathcal{F}_P shows that this choice is not automatic.

title: Sigma-algebras
section: When the required event is not measurable
text:
When the required event is not measurable
A scientific question may require an event that is not measurable under the declared sigma-algebra. This occurs when the analysis asks for the probability of a set that does not belong to \mathcal{F}.
In the example above, an analysis might report a probability for accusative case even though the model measures only number. The problem is not a missing numerical estimate. The accusative set has not been included among the objects that the model can measure.
For the finite examples in this course, taking \mathcal{F}=2^\Omega will usually close the gap. We still write \mathcal{F} separately because the distinction becomes important when the outcome space is not finite.

title: Sigma-algebras
text:
Check your understanding

Start with \{\Omega_4,P\}. Which two events must be added to obtain \mathcal{F}_P?
Is \{\varnothing,\Omega_4\} a sigma-algebra? Check all three requirements.
Why does \{\textit{them}\}\subseteq\Omega_4 not guarantee that \{\textit{them}\}\in\mathcal{F}_P?
Use De Morgan’s law to explain why closure under complements and unions gives closure under intersections.

We have so far built one sigma-algebra by inspection. The next page gives a systematic way to construct the smallest sigma-algebra containing a set of linguistic distinctions.

title: Bayes’ rule
text:
Suppose a pronunciation feature is strongly associated with a small dialect group. Hearing the feature may provide evidence about a speaker’s dialect, but the strength of that evidence cannot be read directly from the rate of the feature within the group. We need to reverse the direction of a conditional probability.
The preceding page gave two applications of the product rule to the same intersection:
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
and
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
Since the left sides are identical, the right sides are equal:
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
If \mathbb{P}(C)>0, divide both sides by \mathbb{P}(C):
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}
       {\mathbb{P}(C)}.
This identity is Bayes’ rule. It is not a new probability axiom. It follows from applying the product rule to one joint event in two orders.

title: Bayes’ rule
text:
Check the derivation with pronouns
Let A again be the accusative event and P the plural event. We want \mathbb{P}(A\mid P). Bayes’ rule gives

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)}
       {\mathbb{P}(P)}.

The values from the joint table are

\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)=\frac{.40}{.70},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(P)=.50.

Substituting them gives

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
&=\frac{(.40/.70)\times.70}{.50}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.50}\\
&=.80.
\end{aligned}

The result matches the direct conditional probability calculation. Bayes’ rule reaches the same quantity from the reversed conditional and the two event probabilities.

title: Bayes’ rule
text:
Work through a dialect feature
Now let D be membership in a dialect group and F be use of a pronunciation feature. Imagine a represented population of 1,000 tokens with these counts.




feature F
no feature F^c
total




dialect group D
90
10
100


other group D^c
180
720
900


total
270
730
1,000



Within the dialect group, the feature is very common:

\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)=\frac{90}{100}=.90.

We want the reversed probability, the probability of group membership given the feature:

\mathbb{P}(D\mid F).

The other required values are

\mathbb{P}(D)=\frac{100}{1000}=.10

and

\mathbb{P}(F)=\frac{270}{1000}=.27.

Bayes’ rule gives

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(D\mid F)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)\mathbb{P}(D)}
        {\mathbb{P}(F)}\\
&=\frac{.90\times.10}{.27}\\
&=\frac{1}{3}.
\end{aligned}

The feature occurs in ninety percent of dialect group tokens, but only one third of all feature tokens come from that group. The group is small, and the feature also occurs outside it. Bayes’ rule incorporates both facts.


Code
p_feature_given_dialect <- .90
p_dialect <- .10
p_feature <- .27

p_dialect_given_feature <-
  p_feature_given_dialect * p_dialect / p_feature

p_dialect_given_feature


The result is approximately .333.

title: Bayes’ rule
section: Read the terms as evidence and prevalence
text:
Read the terms as evidence and prevalence
In the dialect calculation, \mathbb{P}(F\mid D) states how compatible the feature is with the group. The probability \mathbb{P}(D) states how prevalent the group is in the represented population. The denominator \mathbb{P}(F) states how common the feature is overall.
All three quantities are tied to an observation process. A sample balanced to contain equal numbers of speakers from two groups does not directly provide the population value of \mathbb{P}(D). Using the sample proportion would answer a question about the balanced sample unless the design is adjusted to represent the target population.

title: Bayes’ rule
section: A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities
text:
A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities
The error of transposing a conditional probability occurs when \mathbb{P}(F\mid D) is treated as if it were \mathbb{P}(D\mid F). The transposition removes the prevalence term \mathbb{P}(D) and ignores how often F occurs outside D.
A highly characteristic feature may still identify a small share of observed feature tokens when the relevant group is rare. The count table provides a useful check because the reversed conditional can be read directly as 90/270, not 90/100.

title: Bayes’ rule
text:
Check your understanding

Derive Bayes’ rule by equating the two product rule expressions for B\cap C.
In the dialect table, compute \mathbb{P}(F\mid D^c) and \mathbb{P}(D^c\mid F).
Explain in words why .90 and 1/3 answer different questions.
If the dialect group made up half of the represented population while the two within group feature rates stayed fixed, would \mathbb{P}(D\mid F) increase or decrease? Explain without introducing a new formula.

Bayes’ rule reverses a conditional probability while retaining the event prevalences. The next page asks when conditioning does not change a probability at all.

title: Conditional probability
text:
The joint probability \mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40 tells us how much of the full pronoun probability belongs to forms that are both plural and accusative. A different linguistic question asks: among plural forms, how much of the probability belongs to accusative forms?
The phrase among plural forms changes the reference set. We no longer compare the plural accusative mass with the entire sample space. We compare it with the plural event.
This restricted comparison is a conditional probability. We write
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
and read the expression as “the probability of A given P.” The event to the right of the vertical bar states the condition. The event to the left states what we want to measure within that condition.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Rescale the plural event
The plural event contains two outcomes:

P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.

Their original probabilities are .10 and .40. Those values sum to .50, because the plural event receives half of the mass in the full space.



plural outcome
probability in \Omega_4
probability within P




they
.10
.10/.50=.20


them
.40
.40/.50=.80



Dividing each plural probability by .50 makes the two restricted values sum to one. Within the plural event, them receives probability .80. Since them is the only plural accusative outcome,

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Derive the definition
The part of P that also belongs to A is the intersection

A\cap P=\{\textit{them}\}.

Its original probability is .40. The full conditioning event has probability .50. Dividing the relevant part by the conditioning whole gives

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(A\cap P)}{\mathbb{P}(P)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.50}\\
&=.80.
\end{aligned}

In general, for \mathbb{P}(C)>0,

\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.

The numerator finds the part of the condition where B also occurs. The denominator rescales that part relative to all mass in the condition.
This rescaling makes the conditioning event certain within itself:

\mathbb{P}(C\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\cap C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=1.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Reverse the condition
Now ask for the probability of plurality among accusative forms. The numerator is still the same intersection, since P\cap A=A\cap P. The denominator changes:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\mid A)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)}{\mathbb{P}(A)}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.70}\\
&\approx .57.
\end{aligned}

Thus \mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80, while \mathbb{P}(P\mid A)\approx.57. The two expressions use the same overlap but different reference events.
Base R makes the denominator visible.


Code
p_plural_and_acc <- .40
p_plural <- .50
p_acc <- .70

p_acc_given_plural <- p_plural_and_acc / p_plural
p_plural_given_acc <- p_plural_and_acc / p_acc

c(p_acc_given_plural, p_plural_given_acc)


The output is .8 and approximately .571.

title: Conditional probability
section: Why the condition must have positive probability
text:
Why the condition must have positive probability
If \mathbb{P}(C)=0, the original measure places no mass inside C to rescale. The problem is not only arithmetic division by zero. This definition cannot construct a within C probability measure from an event that has no mass.
We will later encounter settings in which conditioning on exact continuous values requires a more careful construction. Nothing from those settings is needed for the finite event calculation here.

title: Conditional probability
section: A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities
text:
A common failure: transposing conditional probabilities
Swapping the target event and conditioning event transposes the conditional probability. A corpus may show that most passive clauses contain an animate subject. This is a claim about

\mathbb{P}(\text{animate subject}\mid\text{passive}).

It does not by itself show that most clauses with animate subjects are passive, which concerns the reversed conditional.
The safest reading procedure is verbal: read the expression from the condition outward. First restrict to the event on the right of the bar. Then ask what portion also belongs to the event on the left.

title: Conditional probability
text:
Check your understanding

Compute \mathbb{P}(A^c\mid P) from the table and verify that it sums with \mathbb{P}(A\mid P) to one.
Compute \mathbb{P}(P\mid A^c) and describe the reference event in words.
Explain why \mathbb{P}(A\mid P) and \mathbb{P}(P\mid A) share a numerator but need not be equal.
Give a linguistic pair of events for which reversing the condition changes the scientific question.

Conditional probability turns an overlap and a reference event into a probability within the conditioning event. The next page rearranges this definition to obtain the product rule.

title: Events
text:
The pronoun sample space lists individual forms, but most linguistic questions concern properties shared by several forms. If we ask whether a recorded pronoun is third person, he, her, and them all give the same answer. We need an object that groups those outcomes without erasing the fact that they are different forms.
An event is a set of outcomes. Let T be the event that the recorded pronoun is third person:
T
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{she},\textit{her},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
The event T occurs whenever the realized outcome belongs to this set. If the outcome is him, then T occurs. If the outcome is we, then T does not occur.
This definition separates two objects.
The same outcome may belong to many events. That fact lets us represent several properties of one token.

title: Events
section: Translate a linguistic question into a set
text:
Translate a linguistic question into a set
Let A be the event that the pronoun has accusative form:

A
=\{\textit{me},\textit{him},\textit{her},\textit{us},\textit{them}\}.

The forms him, her, and them belong to both T and A. We can represent the question “is the pronoun both third person and accusative?” by keeping only those shared outcomes. The relevant operation is intersection:

T\cap A
=\{\textit{him},\textit{her},\textit{them}\}.

Read T\cap A as “T and A.” The intersection is narrower than either starting event because an outcome must satisfy both descriptions.
Now ask whether the pronoun is third person or accusative. We keep every outcome that belongs to at least one of the events. The relevant operation is union:

T\cup A
=\{\textit{me},\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{she},\textit{her},
\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.

Read T\cup A as “T or A.” This or is inclusive. The outcome him belongs to the union even though it belongs to both starting events.
Finally, suppose we ask whether the pronoun is not third person. The complement T^c contains every outcome in \Omega that is not in T:

T^c
=\{\textit{I},\textit{me},\textit{you},\textit{we},\textit{us}\}.

The complement is always relative to the declared sample space. If \Omega included reflexive pronouns, then T^c might include additional forms.

title: Events
text:
Work through one outcome
Take the outcome them.

them belongs to T, so the third person event occurs.
them belongs to A, so the accusative event occurs.
them belongs to T\cap A, since both events occur.
them does not belong to T^c, since the third person event occurs.

Now take me. It belongs to A but not T. It thus belongs to T\cup A, but not to T\cap A.
Base R supplies operations with the same interpretation.


Code
omega <- c("I", "me", "you", "he", "him", "she", "her",
           "we", "us", "they", "them")
third <- c("he", "him", "she", "her", "they", "them")
accusative <- c("me", "him", "her", "us", "them")

intersect(third, accusative)
union(third, accusative)
setdiff(omega, third)


The final expression computes T^c by removing the members of T from \Omega.

title: Events
text:
The two limiting events
The empty event \varnothing contains no outcomes. It cannot occur under the current representation. The full event \Omega contains every outcome, so it occurs whenever the observation process produces a represented result.
These are events because both are subsets of \Omega. They will provide the lower and upper endpoints when we assign probabilities.

title: Events
text:
Translating connectives into set operations
A linguistic connective must be translated into the corresponding set operation. The most common error is translating and with a union or translating inclusive or with an intersection.
Consider the claim “the pronoun is plural and accusative.” A union would include plural nominative they and singular accusative him. Those forms satisfy only half of the claim. The intersection retains only them, which satisfies both parts.
A second source of error is a moving sample space. If T^c is first computed relative to personal pronouns and later interpreted relative to all noun phrases, its meaning has changed. Writing \Omega before computing a complement prevents that shift.

title: Events
text:
Check your understanding

Write T\setminus A, the third person outcomes that are not accusative. Then verify that (T\cap A)\cup(T\setminus A)=T.
Let P=\{\textit{we},\textit{us},\textit{they},\textit{them}\} be the plural event. List P\cap A and P\cup A.
Explain why them can make both T and A occur without being two outcomes.
Suppose reflexives are added to \Omega. Which part of the definition of T^c must be recomputed?

Events give us the questions we might ask. A probability model must also state which of those questions it is prepared to measure. The next page introduces that collection.

title: Independence
text:
Suppose that we learn a pronoun is plural. Does that information change how likely the pronoun is to have accusative form? Conditional probability lets us state the question precisely:
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)\stackrel{?}{=}\mathbb{P}(A).
In the toy pronoun measure,
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70
but
\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)=.80.
Restricting attention to plural forms changes the probability of accusative form. The two events are associated under this measure.
Events B and C are independent when
\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).
This definition compares the observed mass in the intersection with the mass that would result from multiplying the two margins.

title: Independence
section: Check the pronoun events by hand
text:
Check the pronoun events by hand
The marginal probabilities are

\mathbb{P}(P)=.50
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathbb{P}(A)=.70.

Their product is

\mathbb{P}(P)\mathbb{P}(A)
=.50\times.70
=.35.

The observed joint probability is

\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40.

Since .40\neq.35, the events are not independent under this measure.
The same conclusion follows from conditioning. The probability of A changes from .70 in the full space to .80 within P.

title: Independence
text:
Connect the two statements
When \mathbb{P}(C)>0, the product rule gives

\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C).

If B and C are independent, the definition also gives

\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)
=\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C).

Equate the right sides and divide by \mathbb{P}(C):

\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)=\mathbb{P}(B).

Thus independence has a conditional interpretation: learning that C occurred does not change the probability of B.

title: Independence
text:
Build an independent comparison measure
Keep the same outcome labels and margins, but change how the mass is arranged inside the table.

\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)
=.35

Conditioning gives the same result:

\mathbb{P}(A\mid P)
=\frac{.35}{.50}
=.70
=\mathbb{P}(A).

The accusative proportion is also .70 in the singular row. Knowing the number category provides no information about case under this new measure.


Code
joint_independent <- matrix(
  c(.35, .35, .15, .15),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    number = c("plural", "singular"),
    case = c("accusative", "nominative")
  )
)

p_joint <- joint_independent["plural", "accusative"]
p_plural <- sum(joint_independent["plural", ])
p_acc <- sum(joint_independent[, "accusative"])

c(observed = p_joint, product = p_plural * p_acc)


Both returned values are .35.

title: Independence
text:
Independence belongs to the measure
The two tables use the same outcome labels and the same events. The original table makes P and A dependent; the comparison table makes them independent. Independence is thus a property of events under a probability measure, not a property of the linguistic labels alone.
This matters when interpreting corpus data. A construction choice and an animacy feature may appear independent in one genre but associated in another. The sample space may represent the same categories in both cases, while the probability measure changes with the population of tokens.

title: Independence
text:
Independence is not mutual exclusivity
Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together. If two mutually exclusive events B and C both have positive probability, then

\mathbb{P}(B\cap C)=0

while

\mathbb{P}(B)\mathbb{P}(C)>0.

They are not independent. Observing C tells us that B did not occur, which is strong information.
Mutual exclusivity concerns whether the intersection is empty. Independence concerns whether the intersection receives the product of the marginal probabilities.

title: Independence
section: A common failure: no difference means independence
text:
A common failure: no difference means independence
A small difference in a finite sample does not establish independence. Independence is an exact claim about a probability measure. Estimated proportions from finite data will rarely match exactly, even when an independence model is useful, and they may match by chance when the underlying events are associated.
Later chapters introduce statistical models for uncertainty about such claims. At this stage, we can determine only whether a fully specified probability measure satisfies the independence equation.

title: Independence
text:
Check your understanding

Verify independence in the comparison table using both the product definition and the conditional interpretation.
Change the upper left cell from .35 to .40 and the lower left cell from .35 to .30, leaving the margins fixed. Does independence still hold?
Explain why two mutually exclusive events with positive probability cannot be independent.
Give a linguistic setting in which the same two event labels might be independent in one represented population but dependent in another.

This completes the foundations sequence. We have built probability claims from represented outcomes, measurable events, and a coherent measure. Continue to the next module when you are ready to add the next object in the dependency sequence.

title: Joint probability of events
text:
Suppose that we want to know how often a pronoun is both plural and accusative. The word both tells us to find an intersection before doing any probability calculation.
Return to the four form sample space
\Omega_4=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
with the probability measure below.
Let P be the plural event and A the accusative event:
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}
and
A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}.
The joint probability of P and A is the probability assigned to their intersection:
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A).
We will sometimes abbreviate this quantity as \mathbb{P}(P,A). The comma is shorthand for the intersection. It does not introduce another probability operation.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Compute the joint probability by hand
text:
Compute the joint probability by hand
Begin with the set operation:

P\cap A=\{\textit{them}\}.

Then apply the probability measure:

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(P\cap A)
&=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})\\
&=.40.
\end{aligned}

The result says that .40 of the probability mass falls on outcomes that are simultaneously plural and accusative. It does not say that .40 of plural forms are accusative. That second statement restricts the comparison to plural forms and will require conditional probability.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Arrange all joint events in a table
text:
Arrange all joint events in a table
The number distinction P versus P^c and the case distinction A versus A^c divide the sample space into four nonoverlapping intersections.

Read one cell at a time. The upper right cell represents

P\cap A^c=\{\textit{they}\},

so its probability is .10. The lower left cell represents

P^c\cap A=\{\textit{him}\},

so its probability is .30.
The four interior cells are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Their probabilities must sum to one:

.40+.10+.30+.20=1.

The row and column totals are called marginal probabilities because they appear at the margins of the joint table. For instance,

\mathbb{P}(P)=.40+.10=.50.

The marginal probability adds across all case values. It answers how much mass belongs to the plural event without requiring one particular case.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Reconstruct the table in base R
text:
Reconstruct the table in base R
The following code stores the four joint probabilities in a matrix and computes its margins.


Code
joint <- matrix(
  c(.40, .30, .10, .20),
  nrow = 2,
  dimnames = list(
    number = c("plural", "singular"),
    case = c("accusative", "nominative")
  )
)

joint
rowSums(joint)
colSums(joint)
sum(joint)


The row sums are .50 and .50, the column sums are .70 and .30, and the full sum is one. These checks expose a transposed or omitted cell before it affects later calculations.

title: Joint probability of events
text:
Interpret the joint object
A joint probability preserves two distinctions at once. This makes the table more informative than either margin alone. Two corpora can both have \mathbb{P}(P)=.50 and \mathbb{P}(A)=.70 while placing different amounts of mass in P\cap A.
For a linguistic analysis, the joint table is often the first place to inspect whether a proposed association is even present. If plural forms are much more often accusative than singular forms, the relevant difference must appear in how mass is arranged across the four cells, not merely in the two margins.

title: Joint probability of events
section: Using a marginal probability for an intersection
text:
Using a marginal probability for an intersection
A marginal probability cannot replace an intersection probability. In the toy model, \mathbb{P}(A)=.70 includes both him and them. It cannot answer the question about forms that are both plural and accusative because it also includes singular accusative mass.
The repair is grammatical as much as mathematical. Translate and into an intersection, list the outcomes in that intersection, and only then apply \mathbb{P}.

text:
Check your understanding

Compute \mathbb{P}(P^c\cap A^c) by listing the outcomes first.
Explain why \mathbb{P}(P\cap A)=.40 does not mean that 40\% of plural forms are accusative.
