Joint probability measures the overlap in the full sample space. The next page restricts the relevant space to one event and rescales the mass within it.

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Suppose we want to know whether an aspectual mismatch makes a sentence harder to process. We design two conditions and observe the following average reading times at a critical verb:
The mismatch condition is 45 ms slower. What does that difference tell us?
By itself, not very much. Perhaps mismatch caused additional processing. Perhaps the mismatch sentences contained less frequent verbs. Perhaps a small number of participants produced the difference. The subtraction is correct, but its linguistic interpretation depends on how the observations and comparison were constructed.
We will work from the research question to the numerical comparison one step at a time.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Step 1: identify the response
The response is the measurement whose variation we want to understand. In this experiment, it might be reading time at the critical verb.
We need to say more than “reading time.” Is the measurement the first-pass time, total time, or time from a particular reading procedure? Is it recorded in milliseconds or transformed before analysis? Which region supplies it?
A precise statement is:

The response is the total reading time in milliseconds at the critical verb on one participant and sentence trial.

This sentence also identifies the unit of analysis.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Step 2: identify the linguistic contrast
The main predictor distinguishes the observations that the theory says should differ. Here it records whether a trial contains an aspectually matched or mismatched context.
The values must correspond to an actual design contrast. If all matched sentences contain one set of verbs and all mismatched sentences contain another, the predictor does not isolate aspectual mismatch. It also separates the two verb sets.
This is why theoretically interesting predictors are more than available columns. Their values should encode a linguistic distinction for which an account predicts a change in the response.
For a dative-choice study, predictors might encode whether the recipient is pronominal, whether the theme is discourse-new, and how the lengths of the two arguments compare. These variables express proposals about accessibility, information structure, and production difficulty. Trial number or recording channel may also matter, but for a different reason: they describe the design or measurement process.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
section: Step 3: say which observations are being compared
text:
Step 3: say which observations are being compared
Imagine that every participant sees both conditions and every sentence appears in both conditions across participants. The comparison then occurs within participants and within sentence items.
This structure matters. A comparison between different groups of participants may reflect preexisting group differences. A comparison between different item sets may reflect lexical differences. A within-participant and within-item design rules out some of these alternative descriptions by construction.
We can now expand the analysis statement:

The response is total reading time at the critical verb on one participant and sentence trial. The comparison is between aspectually matched and mismatched trials, with both conditions represented within participants and sentence items.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Step 4: state the estimand
The estimand is the population quantity we want to learn about. Let \mu_{\mathrm{mismatch}} be the mean reading time for mismatch trials in the target population, and let \mu_{\mathrm{match}} be the corresponding mean for match trials. One possible estimand is

\tau
=\mu_{\mathrm{mismatch}}
-\mu_{\mathrm{match}}.

In words, \tau is the difference in mean reading time between the mismatch and match conditions.
The population still needs to be specified. Do we mean only these participants and sentences, or new readers and new sentence items from populations represented by the experiment? The design must contain the relevant replication if the broader target is to be plausible.
Our complete statement is now:

One observation is a participant’s reading of the critical verb in one sentence. The response is total reading time in milliseconds. The comparison is the within-participant and within-item contrast between aspectually matched and mismatched contexts. The target is the difference in mean reading time for readers and items from the populations represented by the design.

Writing this statement takes only a few sentences. It prevents the fitted coefficient from acquiring a broader interpretation than the data and design support.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
section: The same records can answer a different question
text:
The same records can answer a different question
Suppose the experiment also asks participants to choose an interpretation after each sentence. We can now ask at least three questions:

Does mismatch change reading time?
Does mismatch change the probability of choosing one interpretation?
Do participants with larger reading-time differences also show larger interpretation differences?

These questions use overlapping records, but their responses and estimands differ. The first has a time response. The second has a categorical response. The third compares participant-level contrasts.
Thus a dataset does not come with one inevitable analysis. The research question determines which observations, response, comparison, and target are relevant.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
What can go wrong?

The unit does not match the claim
Suppose a corpus contains thousands of tokens from one speaker. Those data may describe that speaker’s production precisely. They do not show how speakers vary because only one speaker was observed.


The predictor does not isolate the contrast
Suppose every mismatch sentence uses one set of verbs and every match sentence uses another. The condition difference combines mismatch and lexical identity. Collecting more observations will estimate that combined difference more precisely, but it will not separate the two sources.


The evaluation answers a different question
Suppose a model is meant to predict responses for new readers, but its training and test sets contain trials from the same readers. The evaluation measures prediction of additional trials from observed readers. It does not measure transfer to new readers.
These problems arise before the choice of estimator. A more elaborate model cannot recover a comparison that the data never contained.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Exploration can change the question
Exploratory analysis may show that the original target was poorly chosen. A slider response, for instance, may contain many observations at both endpoints. A target concerned only with average slider position may miss a theoretically important distinction between endpoint and interior responses.
The right response is to write a revised question and target. Exploration is allowed to change the analysis. The change should be explicit so that the new result is not presented as if it answered the original question unchanged.
crumbs: Turning a question into a comparison

title: Turning a question into a comparison
text:
Test the distinction

A corpus study asks whether discourse-new themes favor the prepositional dative. State the unit, response, predictor, comparison, and target.
A study averages acceptability judgments by sentence before analysis but interprets its result as variation among participants. Which variation has already been removed?
A word-recognition model is evaluated by randomly splitting trials, but the intended target is performance on new word types. How should the split change?

On the next page, we apply the same discipline to a famous word-frequency pattern.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Suppose that one observed token is either nominative or accusative under our four form pronoun representation. A single form cannot have both surface cases. We need to distinguish this structural fact about the events from any claim about how frequent the cases are.
Let
N=\{\textit{he},\textit{they}\}
be the nominative event and let
A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}
be the accusative event. The two sets share no outcomes:
N\cap A=\varnothing.
Events whose intersection is empty are mutually exclusive. They cannot both occur on one realization of the outcome represented by \Omega.
The definition concerns set membership:
B\text{ and }C\text{ are mutually exclusive}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
B\cap C=\varnothing.
No probability appears in this definition. We can establish mutual exclusivity before assigning any numerical mass.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Add probabilities across exclusive events
Under the toy probability measure,

\mathbb{P}(N)=.20+.10=.30

and

\mathbb{P}(A)=.30+.40=.70.

Since N and A are mutually exclusive, their union contains two nonoverlapping parts. The probability measure thus gives

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(N\cup A)
&=\mathbb{P}(N)+\mathbb{P}(A)\\
&=.30+.70\\
&=1.
\end{aligned}

In this representation, N\cup A=\Omega_4. The sum equals one because the two events are both exclusive and exhaustive.
Exclusivity and exhaustivity are separate properties. Consider the singleton events \{\textit{he}\} and \{\textit{them}\}. They are mutually exclusive because they share no outcome. Their union does not equal \Omega_4, so their probabilities sum to .20+.40=.60, not to one.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Work through a nonexclusive pair
Let

P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}

be the plural event. Compare P with the accusative event A. Their intersection is

P\cap A=\{\textit{them}\}.

The pair is not mutually exclusive because them makes both events occur. Directly adding \mathbb{P}(P)=.50 and \mathbb{P}(A)=.70 would count the mass on them twice. The result 1.20 is a warning that the nonoverlap condition has failed.
The base R set check should come before the arithmetic.


Code
nominative <- c("he", "they")
accusative <- c("him", "them")
plural <- c("they", "them")

length(intersect(nominative, accusative)) == 0
length(intersect(plural, accusative)) == 0


The first expression returns TRUE; the second returns FALSE.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
The represented outcome matters
Mutual exclusivity is always relative to what happens once. If one outcome is one pronoun token, nominative and accusative forms are mutually exclusive in the toy representation. If one outcome is a sentence containing two pronouns, the event “the sentence contains a nominative pronoun” and the event “the sentence contains an accusative pronoun” may occur together.
The linguistic labels have not changed. The unit represented by one outcome has changed, and that change alters the intersection.

title: Mutually exclusive events
section: Labels do not guarantee mutual exclusivity
text:
Labels do not guarantee mutual exclusivity
Contrasting linguistic labels do not by themselves imply an empty intersection. Terms such as singular and plural often denote mutually exclusive values of one annotation. But terms such as plural and accusative denote values on different dimensions and may overlap.
The safe procedure is to write the events as sets and compute their intersection. If the intersection is empty, the events are mutually exclusive under the declared sample space. The labels alone do not establish the result.

title: Mutually exclusive events
text:
Check your understanding

Are \{\textit{he},\textit{him}\} and \{\textit{they},\textit{them}\} mutually exclusive? Are they exhaustive?
Let F be the first person event and P the plural event in the larger pronoun sample space. Write F\cap P and decide whether the events are mutually exclusive.
Give two mutually exclusive events that are not exhaustive in \Omega_4.
Explain why changing the outcome from one token to one sentence can change whether two linguistic events are mutually exclusive.

Mutual exclusivity tells us when two events cannot occur together. The next page assigns a probability to the event in which two properties do occur together.

title: Probability measures
text:
The sample space \Omega tells us which outcomes the model represents. The sigma-algebra \mathcal{F} tells us which groupings of those outcomes the model can measure. Neither object says that one pronoun form is more common than another.
We add that information with a probability measure. A probability measure assigns a number to each event in \mathcal{F}. We write it as
\mathbb{P}:\mathcal{F}\rightarrow[0,1].
Read this notation from left to right. The function \mathbb{P} takes an event from \mathcal{F} as its input and returns a number between zero and one.
The three objects
\langle\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}\rangle
together form a probability space: represented outcomes, measurable events, and numerical probabilities.

title: Probability measures
text:
Assign mass to individual outcomes
Return to the four pronoun forms

\Omega_4
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.

For this finite example, let \mathcal{F}=2^{\Omega_4} so that every subset is measurable. Suppose a toy corpus motivates these assignments.



outcome
assigned probability




he
.20


him
.30


they
.10


them
.40



The table gives probabilities to singleton events. Larger events receive probabilities by adding the values of their nonoverlapping outcomes.
Let

A=\{\textit{him},\textit{them}\}

be the accusative event. Its probability is

\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A)
&=\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{him}\})
+\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{them}\})\\
&=.30+.40\\
&=.70.
\end{aligned}

The number .70 concerns the event A under this particular measure. It is not a property of the label “accusative” in isolation.

title: Probability measures
text:
The three requirements
Not every numerical assignment is a probability measure. The assignment must satisfy three requirements.
First, every event has nonnegative probability:

\mathbb{P}(B)\geq 0
\qquad\text{for every }B\in\mathcal{F}.

Second, the full sample space has probability one:

\mathbb{P}(\Omega)=1.

Third, probabilities add across a countable collection of events that share no outcomes. If B_1,B_2,\ldots are pairwise disjoint, then

\mathbb{P}\!\left(\bigcup_i B_i\right)
=\sum_i\mathbb{P}(B_i).

The first requirement rules out negative probability. The second says that some represented outcome occurs. The third keeps the probability of a combined event consistent with the probabilities of its nonoverlapping parts.

title: Probability measures
section: Check the toy measure by hand
text:
Check the toy measure by hand
Each value in the table is nonnegative, so the first requirement holds for the singleton events. The singleton events divide \Omega_4 into nonoverlapping parts. Their values sum to

.20+.30+.10+.40=1,

so the probability of \Omega_4 is one.
Now combine he and him. Since the two singleton events share no outcomes,

\mathbb{P}(\{\textit{he},\textit{him}\})
=.20+.30
=.50.

This calculation uses the third requirement. We are not estimating another number from the corpus. We are extending a coherent assignment from individual outcomes to a larger event.
A few base R checks reproduce the arithmetic.


Code
pronoun_mass <- c(he = .20, him = .30, they = .10, them = .40)

all(pronoun_mass >= 0)
sum(pronoun_mass)
sum(pronoun_mass[c("him", "them")])


The three results are TRUE, 1, and .7.

title: Probability measures
text:
Derive two useful consequences
The impossible event has probability zero. Since \Omega and \varnothing are disjoint and \Omega\cup\varnothing=\Omega,

\mathbb{P}(\Omega)
=\mathbb{P}(\Omega)+\mathbb{P}(\varnothing).

Subtracting \mathbb{P}(\Omega) from both sides gives

\mathbb{P}(\varnothing)=0.

The probability of a complement also follows from the requirements. Since B and B^c are disjoint and their union is \Omega,

\mathbb{P}(B)+\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1.

Thus

\mathbb{P}(B^c)=1-\mathbb{P}(B).

For the accusative event, this gives \mathbb{P}(A^c)=1-.70=.30, which agrees with the mass assigned to he and they.

title: Probability measures
section: Assignments that violate the probability axioms
text:
Assignments that violate the probability axioms
An assignment that violates any of the three requirements is not a probability measure. Suppose the four pronoun values were .20, .30, .10, and .50. Each value would lie between zero and one, but their sum would be 1.10. The assignment would give the complete sample space more than unit probability.
Renormalizing the values might produce a probability measure, but it changes every numerical claim. Before doing so, we should ask why the original values did not sum to one. They may be raw corpus counts, percentages computed from different denominators, or model scores that were never intended as probabilities.

Define \(D(\omega)\) as the duration of token \(\omega\).
Then \(D>100\) names the vowel tokens whose durations exceed 100 ms.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
The event \(D>100\) contains \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_3\).
It does not contain the bare numbers 112 and 126.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What must the mapping preserve so that probability statements about its values are defined?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Every measurable set of values must lead back to a measurable event of outcomes.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The preimage of a value set \(E\) is
\[H^{-1}(E)=\{\omega:H(\omega)\in E\}.\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 2.9: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A mapping is measurable when
\[E\in\mathcal G\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H^{-1}(E)\in\mathcal F.\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 2.9: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/02%3A_Probability_Spaces/2.09%3A_Probability_Spaces_Revisited

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If \(H(\omega_1)=1\) and \(H(\omega_2)=H(\omega_3)=2\), what is \(H^{-1}(\{2\})\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[H^{-1}(\{2\})=\{\omega_2,\omega_3\}.\]
The superscript denotes a preimage, not an inverse function.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
A random variable extracts a value without severing that value from the observation process.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Separate values and continuous regions
How probability is arranged over support

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Can the possible values be listed one by one?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A discrete random variable has finite or countably infinite support.

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data
Grammatical person has finite support.
Utterance length has support \(\{0,1,2,3,\ldots\}\).
Both variables are discrete.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Discrete does not mean unordered.
It means that the support values are separate and listable.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A probability mass function, or PMF, assigns probability to each support value:
\[p_S(s)=\mathbb P(S=s).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question



syllables \(s\)
1
2
3
4




\(p_S(s)\)
.42
.33
.17
.08



What is \(\mathbb P(S\geq3)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb P(S\geq3)=.17+.08=.25.\]
The masses are added across disjoint value events.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What changes when a measurement can take any value throughout an interval?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A random variable with a density is absolutely continuous.
A point and an interval are different events.

[Sources]
Pfeiffer, Applied Probability, Distribution and Density Functions: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Applied_Probability_%28Pfeiffer%29/07%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions/7.01%3A_Distribution_and_Density_Functions

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Rounding a duration to whole milliseconds does not make its modeled support discrete.
Storage precision and modeled support answer different questions.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A probability density function, or PDF, represents probability as area:
\[\mathbb P(a\leq X\leq b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Suppose \(f_D(d)=1/100\) on \([50,150]\).
What is \(\mathbb P(80\leq D\leq100)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
Density height is not point probability.
For a continuous variable, \(\mathbb P(D=100)=0\) even when \(f_D(100)>0\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can one representation describe threshold probabilities for either kind of variable?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, is
\[F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\leq x).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
For a discrete variable, the CDF is a step function.
For a continuous variable, it accumulates area under the density through \(x\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Mass belongs to separate values. Density becomes probability only after integration. The CDF accumulates either representation.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Summaries of a distribution
Center, spread, and shape

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can we summarize the center of a distribution while respecting unequal probabilities?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The expected value of a discrete variable is
\[\mathbb E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If word length is 1, 2, or 4 with masses .25, .50, and .25, what is \(\mathbb E[L]\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb E[L]=1(.25)+2(.50)+4(.25)=2.25.\]
An expectation need not be a possible observation.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What if the theoretical quantity is a transformation of the measurement?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Transform first, then average:
\[\mathbb E[g(X)]=\sum_x g(x)p_X(x).\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
In general,
\[\mathbb E[g(X)]\neq g(\mathbb E[X]).\]
The two operations answer different questions.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Must we derive the complete distribution of a sum before finding its expectation?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Linearity of expectation gives
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_i a_iX_i\right]=\sum_i a_i\mathbb E[X_i].\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 4.1: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Linearity of expectation does not require independence.
Dependence changes the distribution of the sum, not this equality.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Challenge
A valid PMF may place enough probability on large values that its expected value is not finite.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data
For \(p_L(l)=6/(\pi^2l^2)\) on \(l=1,2,\ldots\),
\[\mathbb E[L]=\frac{6}{\pi^2}\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{l}.\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Result #1
The harmonic series diverges.
Every finite sample mean is finite, but the model expectation does not exist as a finite number.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can two distributions have the same mean but different dispersion?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The variance is expected squared distance from the mean:
\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Data
\(D_1\) always equals 2.
\(D_2\) equals 1 or 3 with equal probability.
Both means are 2, but their variances are 0 and 1.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can spread be returned to the units of the measurement?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The standard deviation is
\[\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
Standard deviation is a root mean squared distance.
It does not determine how much probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How do variance and directional asymmetry fit within one family of summaries?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The \(k\)th central moment is
\[\mu_k=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^k].\]

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Section 4.1: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.01%3A_Definitions_and_Basic_Properties

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
\(\mu_1=0\). The second central moment is variance. Odd orders retain direction, while even orders do not.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Expectations summarize specified functions of a distribution. Their interpretation depends on existence, units, and the function being averaged.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Discrete distribution families
Models for categories, totals, waiting times, and counts

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can a model assign probabilities to several unordered linguistic categories?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The categorical distribution assigns a probability vector \(\boldsymbol\pi\) to \(K\) labels.
\[\pi_k\geq0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k=1.\]

[Sources]
Stan Functions Reference, Categorical Distribution: https://mc-stan.org/docs/functions-reference/categorical-distribution.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Reordering labels without reordering their probabilities changes the model.
The labels and probability vector must remain aligned.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What is the corresponding model when there are exactly two coded outcomes?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The Bernoulli distribution has support \(\{0,1\}\) and
\[p_Y(y)=\pi^y(1-\pi)^{1-y}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If 1 means a passive response and \(\pi=.30\), what are \(\mathbb P(Y=1)\) and \(\mathbb P(Y=0)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb P(Y=1)=.30,\qquad \mathbb P(Y=0)=.70.\]
Reversing the coding changes which event \(\pi\) names.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How do we model a total number of successes across a fixed number of independent opportunities?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The binomial distribution gives
\[\mathbb P(Y=y)={n\choose y}\pi^y(1-\pi)^{n-y}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
The model requires a fixed number of opportunities, a common success probability, and independent trials conditional on \(\pi\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What changes when tokens are sampled without replacement from a finite corpus list?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The hypergeometric distribution counts samples without replacement from a finite population.

[Sources]
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics, Hypergeometric Distribution: https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/4-5-hypergeometric-distribution

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
Without replacement, one draw changes the composition available for later draws.
The binomial independence assumption no longer applies.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How many opportunities occur before the first target token?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The geometric distribution models a waiting time to the first success.
Its support convention must be stated.

[Sources]
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics, Geometric Distribution: https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/4-4-geometric-distribution

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
If \(Y\) counts trials through the first success, what is \(\mathbb P(Y=3)\)?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[\mathbb P(Y=3)=(1-\pi)^2\pi.\]
Two failures must occur before the success on trial 3.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How many trials occur before the \(r\)th success?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The negative binomial distribution extends the waiting time to a specified success count.
The parameterization must be stated.

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 414, Negative Binomial Distribution: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/lesson/11/11.4

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can we model the number of events observed in a declared amount of exposure?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The Poisson distribution has
\[\mathbb P(Y=y)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!}.\]

[Sources]
Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Count Models: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #4
Exposure is part of the count definition.
Ten events in ten minutes and ten events in ten hours do not express the same rate.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Challenge
The Poisson model makes the mean and variance equal to \(\lambda\).
Observed extra variation signals a model mismatch, not a different calculation of \(\lambda\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Each discrete family corresponds to a different observation process. The support and sampling assumptions identify the relevant family.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Continuous distribution families
Models for bounded and unbounded measurements

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What density assigns equal probability to equal width intervals within fixed bounds?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The continuous uniform distribution on \([a,b]\) has density
\[f_X(x)=\frac{1}{b-a}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
A density height may exceed one.
The total area, not the height, must equal one.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What family can represent different shapes over the open unit interval?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The beta distribution has support \((0,1)\) and shape parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Bayesian Data Analysis: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
\[\mathbb E[X]=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.\]
Holding the ratio fixed while increasing \(\alpha+\beta\) concentrates density around the same mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What family describes a symmetric bell shaped density over the real line?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The normal distribution is determined by location \(\mu\) and scale \(\sigma\).

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Method
Standardize one value with
\[z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}.\]
The resulting value measures distance from the mean in standard deviation units.

[Sources]
Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Standardization: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=102

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Challenge
The normal distribution has support on the complete real line.
It is not automatically appropriate for positive or bounded measurements.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What symmetric reference distribution allows more probability in the tails?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Student’s \(t\) distribution is indexed by degrees of freedom and approaches the normal distribution as they increase.

[Sources]
Winter, Statistics for Linguists, Student’s t Distribution: https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Heavy tails can represent occasional large deviations.
They do not repair an inappropriate response support or measurement model.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What distribution results from adding squared independent standard normal variables?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The chi-squared distribution is indexed by degrees of freedom and has nonnegative support.

[Sources]
OpenStax, Introductory Statistics, Chi-Square Distribution: https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/11-1-facts-about-the-chi-square-distribution

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
With \(
u\) degrees of freedom,
\[\mathbb E[X]=
u,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=2
u.\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
An upper tail probability under a reference distribution is not the probability that a hypothesis is true.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Continuous families differ in support, shape, and tail behavior. Those properties must match the linguistic measurement and observation process.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Simulation
Turning a distribution into reproducible draws

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can one uniform draw select a value from a target distribution?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Inverse transform sampling applies the inverse CDF to \(U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)\).

[Sources]
Peng, Advanced Statistical Computing, Inverse Transform Sampling: https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/inverse-transform-sampling.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Implementation

Compute cumulative probabilities.
Draw \(u\) from the unit interval.
Return the first value whose cumulative probability is at least \(u\).

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
What does a random seed reproduce?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A random seed fixes the initial state of a pseudorandom number generator.
It reproduces one sequence of draws from a procedure.

[Sources]
R base documentation, Random Number Generation: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/Random.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Reproducibility is not validity.
A fixed seed can reproduce a simulation from a poorly specified model.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Upshot
Simulation implements a probability model. The seed makes the implementation repeatable, while the model determines what the draws mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Joint distributions
Probability for paired linguistic measurements

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can a model preserve which duration occurred with which predictability value?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A joint distribution assigns probability to pairs or tuples of random variable values.

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #1
Separate marginal distributions do not recover pairing.
Different joint tables can have the same row and column totals.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How do we recover the distribution of one variable from the joint table?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
A marginal distribution sums over the other variable:
\[p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y).\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
Can two variables be independent within each clause type but associated after clause types are pooled?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
Yes. Conditional independence states independence after conditioning on a third variable.

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
\[X\perp Y\mid Z\]
means
\[p(x,y\mid z)=p(x\mid z)p(y\mid z).\]

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #2
Conditional and unconditional claims differ.
Always state the conditioning set.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How does the expected response change with a specified predictor value?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The conditional expectation is
\[\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].\]
It is a function of the conditioning value \(x\).

[Sources]
Siegrist, Probability, Mathematical Statistics, and Stochastic Processes, Conditional Expected Value: https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/04%3A_Expected_Value/4.07%3A_Conditional_Expected_Value

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #3
The marginal mean combines conditional means using the distribution of the conditioning variable.
Changing that mixture can change the marginal mean without changing either conditional mean.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can paired deviations summarize whether two measurements vary together?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The covariance is
\[\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interpretation
Positive covariance means that above mean values tend to pair with above mean values.
Its magnitude depends on both measurement units.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Question
How can this paired association be expressed without measurement units?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer
The Pearson correlation coefficient is
\[\rho_{XY}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{SD}(X)\operatorname{SD}(Y)}.\]

[Sources]
Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 2: https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Important Point #4
Correlation summarizes linear association.
It does not identify a causal direction.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Interim Discussion
Joint distributions preserve pairing. Marginalization removes one coordinate. Conditioning restricts attention to a specified value or stratum.

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Conclusion
From observations to probability models

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Big Question
What does a probability model say about a linguistic measurement extracted from a complete observation?

title: From outcomes to distributions
text:
Answer

Random variables map outcomes to values while preserving measurable events.
PMFs and PDFs represent probability on different kinds of support.
Expectations summarize declared functions when the relevant expectation exists.
Distribution families encode particular observation processes.
Joint distributions retain relations among several measurements.

text:

Before choosing a distribution, what are the outcome, the measured value, its support, and the process that generated it?
