title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Thirty Rochester speakers each produce twenty vowel tokens.
The table has 600 rows and 30 sampled speakers.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Approach
Buchstaller and Khattab ask how a sample of speakers can support a claim about a speech community.
Buchstaller and Khattab 2013

[Sources]
https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139013734.006

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A target population contains the units about which we want to make a claim.
A sample contains the units observed through a particular selection process.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Goal
A parameter is a fixed numerical feature of the modeled population.
The realized sample mean is an estimate.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-1-definitions-of-statistics-probability-and-key-terms

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Six hundred tokens can sharpen summaries for 30 observed speakers. They do not create 600 independently sampled speakers.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Independent sampling
Connecting observations to a parameter

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Four clauses are coded for whether each contains an overt subject.
\[
(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(1,0,1,1)
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Observations are independent and identically distributed (IID) when they share one distribution and their joint probability factors.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
X_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi),\qquad
p(x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid\pi)=\prod_i p(x_i\mid\pi).
\]
Recall the Bernoulli distribution.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
For the observed sequence,
\[
p(1,0,1,1\mid\pi)=\pi^3(1-\pi).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Distinct rows need not be independent. Clauses can share speakers, documents, genre, and discourse context.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
A corpus proportion
Making the sampling statement concrete

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
The Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank teaching extract contains 12,280 personal pronoun tokens.
UD English EWT

[Sources]
https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/en_ewt/

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
Accusative tokens: \(3{,}327\)
Nonaccusative tokens: \(8{,}953\)
\[
\widehat\pi=\frac{3327}{12280}\approx.271
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
The estimate describes the coded extract. It does not explain case licensing or justify independence across repeated documents and forms.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Maximum likelihood
Comparing parameter values for fixed data

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
Which accusative probability makes the observed token sequence most probable under the working model?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The likelihood function holds the observed data fixed and varies the parameter.
\[
L(\pi;\mathbf x)=\pi^{3327}(1-\pi)^{8953}
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
\(p(x\mid\pi)\) is a distribution over possible observations for fixed \(\pi\).
\(L(\pi;\mathbf x)\) compares parameter values for fixed observations.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The log likelihood turns a product into a sum.
\[
\ell(\pi)=k\log\pi+(n-k)\log(1-\pi)
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The maximum-likelihood estimate maximizes the likelihood.
\[
\widehat\pi_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\frac{k}{n}=.271
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Maximum likelihood selects a parameter value under the declared model. It does not establish that the model is adequate.

title: Learning from a sample
section: Maximum likelihood for a Poisson mean
text:
Maximum likelihood for a Poisson mean
A count response

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
The English Web Treebank teaching extract contains 2,594 wh expressions and their linear distances to annotated heads.
Silveira et al. 2014

[Sources]
https://universaldependencies.org/treebanks/en_ewt/index.html
https://aclanthology.org/L14-1067/

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\),
\[
\ell(\lambda)=\left(\sum_i x_i\right)\log\lambda-n\lambda-\sum_i\log(x_i!).
\]
Recall the Poisson distribution.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
Setting the derivative to zero gives
\[
\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\bar x\approx3.007.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
The distance data exclude zero, and the Poisson mean variance equality may fail.
Estimation and adequacy are separate questions.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Sampling distributions
An estimation rule across possible samples

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A lexical decision task has population accuracy \(\pi=.75\).
Each possible sample produces a different sample proportion.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The sampling distribution is the probability distribution of an estimator across possible samples.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The parameter is fixed, the estimator is a rule, and the estimate is that rule’s value for one realized sample.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Result #1
Larger independent samples concentrate the sampling distribution around the same parameter.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
A sampling distribution contains possible estimates, not possible population parameters.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Standard errors
The spread of a sampling distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
How much would an estimate vary across repeated samples under the model?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The standard error is the standard deviation of an estimator’s sampling distribution.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For an IID sample mean,
\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Result #1
Doubling \(n\) does not halve the standard error. Multiplying \(n\) by four does.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Replacing the true independent unit with the row count makes the standard error too small.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Estimator bias
Average error across possible samples

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The bias of an estimator is
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat\theta)=E[\widehat\theta]-\theta.
\]

[Sources]
https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/07%3A_Point_Estimation/7.01%3A_Estimators

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
An unbiased estimator may miss the parameter in one realized sample.
Realized error is not estimator bias.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Unbiasedness alone does not rank estimators. Their sampling variation may differ.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Mean squared error
Combining bias and sampling variance

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Mean squared error averages squared estimation error.
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\theta)=E[(\widehat\theta-\theta)^2]
\]

[Sources]
https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/07%3A_Point_Estimation/7.01%3A_Estimators

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat\theta)
=\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\theta)
+\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat\theta)^2.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Surprising Fact
A slightly biased estimator can have lower MSE if its sampling variance is sufficiently smaller.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Bias and variance answer different questions. MSE evaluates their combined squared error.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Confidence intervals
Coverage across repeated samples

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Goal
Estimate a population prominence contrast \(\tau\) from one realized study.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A confidence interval is produced by a procedure with a declared repeated sampling coverage probability.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
An approximate normal interval is
\[
\widehat\tau\pm1.96\operatorname{SE}(\widehat\tau).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The coverage probability is the probability that the interval procedure contains the fixed parameter across repeated samples.

[Sources]
https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson09

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Confidence is a property of the interval procedure. It is not a posterior probability attached to the fixed parameter.

title: Learning from a sample
section: Exact intervals for a binomial probability
text:
Exact intervals for a binomial probability
When the normal interval is unreliable

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
A Wald interval can extend outside zero and one and can have poor coverage for small samples or probabilities near a boundary.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The Wald interval uses a normal approximation around the sample proportion.

[Sources]
https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson02

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Approach
The Clopper-Pearson confidence interval inverts exact binomial tail tests.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/binom.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
“Exact” refers to the finite sample binomial calculation. It does not establish independence, a shared probability, or representative sampling.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Bootstrap confidence intervals
Approximating a sampling distribution by resampling

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Twelve speakers supply median fundamental frequency measurements.
The target is the population median.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The nonparametric bootstrap resamples observations with replacement from the empirical distribution.

[Sources]
https://openintro-ims.netlify.app/foundations-bootstrapping.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method

Sample twelve speakers with replacement.
Calculate the bootstrap median.
Repeat the resampling procedure.
Use the distribution of bootstrap medians.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A percentile bootstrap confidence interval uses quantiles of the bootstrap estimates.

[Sources]
https://openintro-ims.netlify.app/foundations-bootstrapping.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
If tokens repeat within speakers, resample speakers and retain each selected speaker’s tokens together.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
The resampling unit must match the independent unit in the population claim.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Null hypotheses and test statistics
Comparing a discrepancy with a reference distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A null hypothesis states a parameter claim. An alternative hypothesis states the competing parameter values.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
A test statistic standardizes the observed discrepancy.
\[
T=\frac{\widehat\theta-\theta_0}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\theta)}
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The null distribution is the reference distribution of the test statistic under the null model.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
A p value measures tail compatibility with the declared null model. It is not an effect size or the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Inference for one mean
Unknown response variance

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Each independent speaker supplies one acoustic contrast.
The target is the population mean contrast \(\mu\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The one-sample t-test uses the estimated standard error of the sample mean.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=308

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
t=\frac{\bar X-\mu_0}{S/\sqrt n},
\qquad df=n-1.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
A t confidence interval replaces the normal critical value with the corresponding t quantile.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Many tokens from one speaker do not provide many independent speaker contrasts.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Paired observations
Constructing a within pair response

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Every speaker produces two vowel categories.
The measurements share vocal tract anatomy and recording conditions.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A paired design forms one within pair difference for each independent pair.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=173

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
D_s=Y_{sA}-Y_{sB}.
\]
Shared additive speaker shifts cancel inside \(D_s\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Covariance determines the precision gained by pairing.
Positive within pair covariance reduces the variance of the difference.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Sorting the two response vectors independently destroys the pairing and can create invalid differences.

title: Learning from a sample
section: Inference for a paired mean difference
text:
Inference for a paired mean difference
Applying the one sample procedure to differences

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Goal
Estimate the population mean of the speaker differences, \(\mu_D\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The paired t-test is a one-sample t-test applied to \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\).
\[
t=\frac{\bar D-\mu_{D,0}}{S_D/\sqrt n}
\]

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=308

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Speaker F1 differences use the vowel measurements of Hillenbrand et al.
Hillenbrand et al. 1995

[Sources]
https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
The interval describes the mean within speaker vowel contrast, not the distribution of individual vowel measurements.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Comparing two independent means
Different units in each group

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
How does uncertainty change when the two condition means come from different speakers?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Welch’s two-sample t-test allows the two groups to have different variances.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/t.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar X_1-\bar X_2)
=\sqrt{\frac{S_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{S_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Do not use an equal variance assumption merely because a software default or familiar formula includes it.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Paired and independent designs use different sources of variation. The test must match the design.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Fisher’s exact test
A conditional comparison for a two by two table

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A morphological sample classifies nouns by stem type and plural allomorph.
The question is whether the two classifications are independent.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Fisher’s exact test constructs a conditional null distribution over tables with the observed margins fixed.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/fisher.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The free cell follows a hypergeometric distribution under the conditional independence model.
The two sided p value sums tables at least as improbable as the observed table.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
The two sided p value is approximately \(.0391\).
The observed table probability is only one term in that sum.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The sample odds ratio describes the direction and magnitude of association in the observed table.

[Sources]
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/fisher.test.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Association between stem type and allomorph does not identify a causal or linguistic mechanism.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
The chi-squared test of independence
An approximate reference distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A corpus classifies 300 referring expressions by grammatical role and form.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The chi-squared test of independence compares observed cell counts with counts expected under independence.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-business-statistics-2e/pages/11-4-test-of-independence

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For cell \(r,c\),
\[
E_{rc}=\frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{grand total}}.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
\[
X^2=\sum_{r,c}\frac{(O_{rc}-E_{rc})^2}{E_{rc}},
\qquad df=(r-1)(c-1).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Interpretation
The omnibus statistic records aggregate discrepancy. Signed cell differences locate its direction.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Small expected counts weaken the approximation. Repeated speakers or documents also violate the independent row assumption.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Posterior distributions
Updating uncertainty about a parameter

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A listener chooses a collective or distributive interpretation for an ambiguous reciprocal sentence.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A prior distribution assigns probability to parameter values before the present data are observed.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Multiply prior support by likelihood support and normalize.
\[
p(\theta\mid y)=\frac{p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)}{p(y)}
\]
Recall Bayes’ rule.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The posterior distribution represents parameter uncertainty after conditioning on the observed data.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The posterior is a probability distribution over the parameter. The likelihood alone is not.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Summarizing posterior draws
Claims from a posterior distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A posterior summary is a numerical description calculated from the posterior distribution or its draws.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
Posterior means and medians locate the center.
Credible intervals retain a declared posterior probability mass.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For a directional claim, estimate
\[
P(\theta>0\mid y)\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mathbf 1(\theta^{(s)}>0).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Transform and contrast parameters inside each draw before summarizing. This preserves joint posterior uncertainty.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Conjugate priors
An analytic beta Bernoulli update

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A phonological study observes 14 word final coronal stop deletions and 6 realized stops.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A conjugate prior yields a posterior in the same distribution family after multiplication by the likelihood.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
\Pi\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),\qquad
Y\mid\Pi=\pi\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,\pi).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
\[
\Pi\mid y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha+s,\beta+f).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Interpretation
The shape parameters admit a pseudocount interpretation for the algebra. They are not literal unobserved tokens.

[Sources]
https://web.stanford.edu/group/sisl/public/dmu.pdf

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Prior predictive distributions
Checking implications before observing the present data

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
What response counts does the complete prior model expect for ten ambiguous sentences?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The prior predictive distribution averages the observation model over the prior.
\[
p(\widetilde y)=\int p(\widetilde y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Draw one parameter value for a complete simulated dataset, then generate the responses conditional on that value.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Interpretation
Inspect predictions on the response scale. Ask whether the implied counts are plausible before using the present responses.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Drawing a new response probability for every trial represents a different sampling structure from drawing one for the complete ten trial dataset.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Posterior predictive distributions
Predicting after the update

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The posterior predictive distribution averages the observation model over posterior uncertainty.
\[
p(\widetilde y\mid y)=\int p(\widetilde y\mid\theta)p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Draw \(\theta^{(s)}\) from the posterior, then draw \(\widetilde y^{(s)}\) from the observation model conditional on \(\theta^{(s)}\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Predictive spread contains parameter uncertainty and future response variation.
These are distinct sources of variation.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #2
Prediction asks what future observations may look like. Model checking compares replicated observations with the observed data.

title: Learning from a sample
section: When the posterior will not normalize by hand
text:
When the posterior will not normalize by hand
The computational problem

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Four standardized closure duration contrasts use a nonconjugate prior and normal observation model.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The normalizing constant is
\[
Z=\int p(y\mid\theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta.
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introBDA.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The unnormalized posterior still gives relative support because \(Z\) does not depend on \(\theta\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Computational difficulty does not imply broad posterior uncertainty. A concentrated posterior can still have an intractable normalizer.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Question
How can we calculate posterior expectations without evaluating every possible parameter value?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Monte Carlo integration
Replacing an expectation with a sample average

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Monte Carlo integration approximates an expectation with independent draws from the target distribution.
\[
E_p[h(\Theta)]\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}h(\theta^{(s)})
\]

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Probabilities are expectations of indicator functions.
\[
P(\Theta>0)=E[\mathbf 1(\Theta>0)]
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Monte Carlo error is variation caused by using a finite number of simulation draws.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
More simulation draws reduce Monte Carlo error. They do not reduce posterior uncertainty.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Importance sampling
Sampling from a different distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Direct draws from the target distribution may be unavailable.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Approach
Draw from a proposal distribution \(q\) and reweight the draws toward the target \(p\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The importance weight is
\[
w(\theta)=\frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)}.
\]

[Sources]
https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/inverse-problems-and-data-assimilation/monte-carlo-sampling-and-importance-sampling/AEE4AC4E63548DC6A732013B571841D8

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
E_p[h(\Theta)]=E_q[w(\Theta)h(\Theta)]
\]
when the target is normalized and the proposal covers its support.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
A few very large weights can dominate the estimate. Proposal draws are frequent under \(q\), not under \(p\).

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Markov chains
Dependent simulation draws

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A Markov chain makes the next state depend on the current state, conditional on which earlier states add no information.

[Sources]
https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/markov-chain-monte-carlo.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
P(X_{t+1}=x\mid X_t,\ldots,X_0)=P(X_{t+1}=x\mid X_t).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A distribution is stationary when one transition leaves it unchanged.

[Sources]
https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/markov-chain-monte-carlo.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Irreducibility permits movement between relevant states. Aperiodicity prevents deterministic cycling.

[Sources]
https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/markov-chain-monte-carlo.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Markov chain Monte Carlo
Using a chain to approximate a target distribution

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the target.

[Sources]
https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/markov-chain-monte-carlo.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
After the chain reaches its stationary regime,
\[
E_p[h(\Theta)]\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}h(\theta^{(s)}).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The posterior, the chain’s state distribution at iteration \(t\), and the empirical distribution of saved draws are different objects.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Correct stationary distribution does not guarantee efficient exploration in a finite run.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Metropolis-Hastings sampling
Propose, compare, and accept

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm corrects proposal moves with an acceptance probability.

[Sources]
https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/advstatcomp/markov-chain-monte-carlo.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Implementation

Propose \(\theta'\) from \(q(\theta'\mid\theta)\).
Calculate the acceptance probability.
Accept the proposal or repeat the current state.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
\alpha=\min\left(1,
\frac{\widetilde p(\theta')q(\theta\mid\theta')}
{\widetilde p(\theta)q(\theta'\mid\theta)}
\right).
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The unknown normalizing constant cancels from the target density ratio.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
A proposal that is too narrow moves slowly. A proposal that is too wide is rejected often.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
Using gradients to propose distant states

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) augments the parameter with momentum and follows a numerically approximated Hamiltonian trajectory.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Potential energy is the negative log target density. Kinetic energy is determined by momentum and the mass matrix.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The Hamiltonian is the sum of potential and kinetic energy.
The gradient directs movement along high density regions.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Implementation
The leapfrog integrator alternates momentum and position updates.
A Metropolis correction accounts for numerical error.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
HMC uses local gradient information to make long proposals with high acceptance probability.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Mass matrices and posterior geometry
Matching movement to scale and correlation

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The mass matrix determines the kinetic energy and maps momentum into parameter velocity.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
\[
K(p)=\frac{1}{2}p^\top M^{-1}p.
\]
A suitable \(M\) adjusts movement to posterior scales and correlations.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Output
A unit mass matrix uses one scale for every direction. A diagonal matrix adapts scales. A dense matrix also adapts correlations.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Stan learns the mass matrix during warmup. The learned geometry changes computation, not the model’s posterior target.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
The No-U-Turn Sampler
Choosing a trajectory length

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) builds an HMC trajectory and stops extending it when the path begins to reverse.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Grow a balanced trajectory tree, check the turning condition, and select one valid state from the path.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
NUTS chooses trajectory length. Warmup separately adapts step size and the mass matrix.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Stopping at the first rejected leapfrog point would bias the trajectory. NUTS selects from a valid constructed path.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Implementing a model in Stan
Translating a factorization into a program

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Stan is a probabilistic programming language that uses gradient based MCMC for continuous parameter models.

[Sources]
https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-introstan.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Implementation

Declare observed data and their constraints.
Declare unknown parameters and their constraints.
Add prior and likelihood contributions to the target density.
Supply a matching data object.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
The model block should match the declared joint factorization.
Parameter constraints imply transformations and Jacobian adjustments handled by Stan.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
A program can compile and sample from the model that was coded while the model remains inappropriate for the linguistic data.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Reading trace plots
Visual evidence about chain behavior

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A trace plot displays saved parameter draws against iteration for each chain.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/articles/plotting-mcmc-draws.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Look for stable location, overlap across chains, repeated crossing, and continued movement.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Drift indicates nonstationarity. Separated chains indicate incomplete exploration or distinct regions.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Overlapping traces do not prove convergence. They provide one diagnostic view that must agree with numerical summaries.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Cross chain agreement
Comparing within and between chain variation

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The rank-normalized split \(\widehat R\) statistic compares variation within chains with variation between split chains after rank normalization.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/rstan/reference/Rhat.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Interpretation
\(\widehat R\) near one indicates that the chains have similar location and scale for the monitored parameter.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Chains can agree inside the same incomplete region. \(\widehat R\) is not a certificate that the posterior was fully explored.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Inspect the largest \(\widehat R\) across all reported and scientifically relevant parameters, not one convenient coefficient.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Autocorrelation in a Markov chain
Dependence across saved iterations

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Autocorrelation is correlation between draws separated by a fixed lag within one stationary chain.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The autocorrelation function reports autocorrelation across lags.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Autocorrelation can reduce Monte Carlo efficiency even when the chain has the correct stationary distribution.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Thinning discards draws and usually does not improve estimation for a fixed computational run.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Effective sample size
Information in dependent draws

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Effective sample size is the number of independent draws that would provide comparable Monte Carlo precision.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For one stationary chain,
\[
N_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{N}{1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho_t}.
\]

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
Bulk ESS concerns central posterior summaries. Tail ESS concerns quantiles and tail probabilities.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/diagnostics-warnings.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
Effective sample size counts information in simulation draws. It does not count speakers, items, or experimental observations.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Divergent Hamiltonian transitions
Numerical failure in difficult geometry

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A divergent transition occurs when numerical integration error becomes too large along an HMC trajectory.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/mcmc.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
A positive scale parameter and latent deviations can create a narrow, highly curved posterior region.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Locate divergent draws in parameter space. Then reconsider parameterization, scale, prior information, and model geometry.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Discarding divergent draws changes the empirical distribution and does not repair the sampler’s failure to explore the target.

title: Learning from a sample
section: Reading pairs plots of posterior draws
text:
Reading pairs plots of posterior draws
Locating difficult posterior geometry

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A pairs plot displays pairwise projections of posterior draws.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/bayesplot/articles/plotting-mcmc-draws.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Inspect funnels, narrow ridges, strong correlations, multimodal separation, and the locations of divergent draws.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
A geometric association between parameters does not show that one parameter causes the other.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Pairs plots connect a sampler warning with the posterior region where computation is difficult.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Generating derived quantities in Stan
Calculating within posterior draws

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
The generated quantities block computes derived values or simulations after each saved parameter draw.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/reference-manual/blocks.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
Compute a deterministic contrast within each draw to preserve joint uncertainty.
Simulate a replicated response when the quantity is stochastic.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #1
The block does not change the posterior target because its calculations occur after parameter sampling.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Important Point #2
Preserve participant, item, and observation indices when simulated quantities must retain the fitted dependence structure.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Posterior predictive checks
Comparing observations with replicated data

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A posterior predictive check compares observed data with replicated data generated under posterior draws.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/posterior-predictive-checks.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Method
For each posterior draw, generate \(\widetilde y^{(s)}\) from the observation model using the same design and indexing as the observed data.
Recall the posterior predictive distribution.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer
A discrepancy function reduces observed and replicated data to a feature the model should reproduce.

[Sources]
https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/posterior-predictive-checks.html

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Data
Compare observed and replicated variance, endpoint mass, group means, lexical tails, or another theory bearing feature.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Challenge
Checking only a statistic that the fitted model must reproduce closely can miss failures elsewhere in the distribution.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Interpretation
A mismatch identifies a feature the fitted model fails to reproduce. Agreement does not establish that the model is true.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Conclusion
What inference adds

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Big Question
What can observed speakers, tokens, items, or measurements tell us beyond the realized sample?

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Answer

Frequentist procedures describe estimator behavior across possible samples.
Bayesian procedures represent uncertainty with posterior distributions.
Simulation approximates posterior expectations and predictions.
Diagnostics assess finite computation and model adequacy separately.

title: Learning from a sample
text:
Upshot
Every inferential result must identify its population target, sampling model, procedure, and evidence that the computation and fitted model are adequate.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Big Question
How well does a fitted model predict linguistic observations that did not contribute to its fit?

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Data
A reading-time corpus repeats readers, passages, sentences, and word positions. A new row is not necessarily a new reader or a new passage.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Challenge
Training fit rewards a model for adapting to the responses it has already seen. It does not measure prediction for omitted responses.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
This Module

State what must be new at prediction time.
Choose a loss and a validation split.
Compare models on matched omitted observations.
Relate predictive evaluation to likelihood-based criteria.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
section: What must be new at prediction time
text:
What must be new at prediction time
Naming the omitted observations

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Question
Does the claim concern another response from represented units, a new participant, a new item, or a new passage?

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Answer
Out-of-sample prediction evaluates responses omitted during fitting. The omitted unit must match the claim.

Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 14

Defining the cost of an error

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Question
Should a 40 ms miss count twice as much as a 20 ms miss, or four times as much?

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Answer
Squared-error loss gives the 40 ms miss four times the loss. Absolute-error loss gives it twice the loss.

https://wanghemath.github.io/Book-ProbabilityStatisticalTheory/chapters/chapter-13-point-estimation2.html

Prediction bias and prediction variance
Error across repeated training samples

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Surprising Fact
A flexible curve may follow the true frequency effect more closely on average while changing much more across possible corpora.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Method
The bias-variance decomposition applies the earlier ideas of estimator bias and estimator variance to predictions.
\[
\mathbb{E}(Y-\widehat f(x))^2
=\sigma^2+\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat f(x))^2+\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f(x))
\]

James et al., Chapter 2


[Sources]

https://www.statlearning.com/s/ISLRSeventhPrinting.pdf

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Upshot
Bias and prediction variance describe a complete learning procedure over repeated training samples. One observed corpus does not separately identify them.
Return to the notes

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Training and test data
Separating fitting from evaluation

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Idea
The training set determines every fitted quantity. The test set is used only to evaluate the fitted procedure.

Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Section 5.9


[Sources]

https://otexts.com/fpp3/training-test.html

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Challenge
Data leakage occurs when test information influences a fitted decision. Centering, selection, and imputation must therefore be estimated within training data.

scikit-learn, Common pitfalls


[Sources]

https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Upshot
Split first. Then estimate every response-adaptive step on the training set and evaluate the prespecified procedure once on the test set.
Return to the notes

Cross-validation
Rotating the separation

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Method
K-fold cross-validation (CV) divides the data into folds and rotates which fold supplies the omitted responses.

Nicenboim, Schad, and Vasishth, Chapter 14


[Sources]

https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-cv.html

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Implementation

Fit the complete procedure outside fold \(k\).
Predict the responses in fold \(k\).
Store predictions in their original rows.
Repeat until every row has one omitted-data prediction.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Upshot
Cross-validation estimates the performance of the complete procedure. Every fitted transformation and selection decision belongs inside the rotation.
Return to the notes

Comparing predictive loss
Pairing models on the same omitted groups

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Method
For each held-out group \(g\), compare paired losses with
\[
\Delta_g=L_{g,A}-L_{g,B}.
\]
Positive values favor Model B.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Interpretation
Report the aggregate difference, the proportion of groups that improve, and the distribution of group differences. Fold means are not independent replications.

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:

A coefficient and a held-out loss difference answer different questions. The first describes a fitted association. The second describes predictive contribution under the chosen split.

Comparing nested likelihoods
Likelihood-ratio tests

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Question
Does a larger model improve maximized likelihood enough to reject the restrictions imposed by a nested smaller model?

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Method
The likelihood-ratio test (LRT) uses
\[
D=2\{\ell(\widehat\theta_1)-\ell(\widehat\theta_0)\}.
\]

Winter, Chapter 15


[Sources]

https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=261

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Upshot
The test concerns a specified nested restriction under its reference conditions. It is not an estimate of out-of-sample predictive performance.
Return to the notes

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Penalizing in-sample fit
Information criteria

title: Prediction beyond the fitted data
text:
Method
Akaike information criterion (AIC) combines maximized fit with a parameter-count penalty.
\[
\mathrm{AIC}=-2\ell(\widehat\theta)+2k
\]

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Big Question
What must a design do before a model can estimate the intended linguistic comparison?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
An experiment compares recognition after familiar and unfamiliar accent training.
Each participant completes 40 trials.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Surprising Fact
Twenty four participants produce 960 rows, but training was assigned only 24 times.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
A model cannot create condition assignments, item balance, or retained observations that the design did not produce.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
This Module

Identify the unit and mechanism of assignment.
Choose a participant structure that preserves the manipulation.
Distribute item versions across participants.
Declare exclusions and evaluate the complete procedure by simulation.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Idea
Winter begins with repeated linguistic observations and asks which observations may count as independent evidence.
Winter 2020, Sections 14.2 and 14.3

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Units of assignment
What can independently receive a condition?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
Does accent training vary across participants or across recognition trials?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
The unit of assignment is the entity that can independently receive a condition.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
The unit of observation is the entity represented by one measured response.
Recall the unit of analysis.

[Sources]
https://bookdown.org/pkaldunn/Book/UnitsObsAnalysis.html

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Ask what could have received a different condition under the actual procedure.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Twelve trial rows from four participants contain twelve observations and four assignment units.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
A classroom receives one teaching method. Each student gives five responses.
What is assigned, and what is observed?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Additional trials may improve measurement. They do not add independent condition assignments.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Random assignment
How conditions reach assignment units

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
If participants choose the accent condition, prior accent experience may differ between conditions.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
The assignment mechanism is the probability rule that selects a condition for each assignment unit.

[Sources]
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Under independent assignment with equal probabilities,
\[
P(Z_i=1)=P(Z_i=0)=.5.
\]

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Surprising Fact
A valid mechanism can produce a realized split of three participants and five participants.
Balance is an expectation, not a guarantee for one sample.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Approach
Restricted random assignment samples only from assignments that satisfy a declared balance condition.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #1
Random sampling concerns entry into the study.
Random assignment concerns allocation of conditions within the study.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #2
Save the realized assignment table and conceal future assignments from recruiters.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Within-participant designs
Each participant supplies a contrast

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
Participants differ in their use of a seven point acceptability scale.
Stable response habits may obscure a construction contrast.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
In a within-participant design, each participant contributes observations to more than one condition.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Each participant supplies a difference.
\[
D_i=Y_{i1}-Y_{i0},\qquad \bar D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_iD_i
\]
Recall paired observations.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Four active minus passive differences are \(1\), \(2\), \(1\), and \(0\).
Their mean is one scale point.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
A carryover effect occurs when an earlier condition changes a later response.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
If every active sentence precedes its passive counterpart, what two explanations are combined in the condition difference?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Stable participant shifts may cancel, but order and lasting effects remain part of the design.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Between-participant designs
Comparing groups

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
Accent training changes a listener. The original untrained state cannot be restored.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
In a between-participant design, each participant contributes observations to only one condition.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
The comparison is between group means.
\[
\widehat\Delta=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0
\]
Recall independent means.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Familiar training mean: \(.800\)
Unfamiliar training mean: \(.715\)
Estimated difference: \(.085\)

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
Sorting two group vectors and pairing their rows invents a relation that the design never created.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Use a between-participant design when the manipulation cannot be repeated without changing its meaning.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Counterbalancing
Distributing item versions

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
How can each item appear in every condition without showing every participant every version?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
Counterbalancing distributes item versions across lists so that condition is not tied to item identity.

[Sources]
https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method



item
list 1
list 2




A
condition 1
condition 2


B
condition 2
condition 1

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #1
The list map must be assigned to participants by a recorded procedure.
A balanced file does not show that lists reached participants appropriately.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Important Point #2
Counterbalancing distributes condition versions. It does not make responses from the same participant or item independent.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
After exclusions, condition 1 has fewer observations for one item.
Is the collected dataset still balanced?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Exclusion rules
Defining the analyzed set

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
A microphone failure and a 4,000 millisecond response both look unusual.
Only one is necessarily a missing measurement.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Approach
Let \(R_i=1\) when observation \(i\) is retained and \(R_i=0\) when it is excluded.
The retained analysis conditions on \(R_i=1\).

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
All five grammatical trials return responses.
Two of five ungrammatical trials time out.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Result #1
Among retained trials, the mean difference is only 10 milliseconds.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Result #2
The timeout rate is zero in one condition and forty percent in the other.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Interpretation
The retained mean describes trials that produced a response before timeout.
It does not show that the manipulation had little effect.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method
Define rules before inspecting the desired contrast. Report participant and trial flow, reasons for removal, and exclusions by every relevant condition and group.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Exclusion helps define the estimand. It is not merely table cleaning.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Power by simulation
Evaluating the complete planned procedure

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Question
How many participants are needed for a within-participant acceptability experiment?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
There is no answer until we specify a data-generating process and a decision rule.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Data
For participant differences,
\[
D_i\sim\operatorname{Normal}(\delta,\sigma_D).
\]

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Method

Generate the exact planned design.
Apply the planned exclusions.
Fit the planned analysis.
Apply the planned decision rule.
Repeat the complete procedure.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Output
Estimated power is the proportion of simulated studies that meet the decision rule under the stated generating process.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer
A power curve shows estimated power across participant counts or effect assumptions.

[Sources]
https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=187

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Challenge
Increasing the number of simulations reduces simulation error. It does not add participants to the planned study.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
Power is conditional on the assumed process, complete design, analysis, and decision rule.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Conclusion
Design before analysis

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Big Question
What must a design do before a model can estimate the intended linguistic comparison?

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Answer

Count assignments at the level where conditions can vary.
Match participant structure to the manipulation.
Counterbalance item versions and record list assignment.
Treat retention as part of the estimand.
Simulate the complete planned procedure.

title: Designing linguistic comparisons
text:
Upshot
A statistical model begins after the design has already determined which comparisons the data can support.

title: Factorization
text:
Big Question
Can several linguistic measurements be represented by a smaller number of recurring numerical patterns?

title: Factorization
text:
Data
A vowel token may have F1, F2, F3, duration, and voice quality measurements.
A verb may have frequencies for more than one hundred syntactic frames.

title: Factorization
text:
Challenge
The columns may share structure, but a lower dimensional representation is meaningful only with respect to a declared matrix and reconstruction task.

title: Factorization
text:
This Module

Define rows, columns, origins, and units.
Build one rank one pattern.
Order several patterns with the singular value decomposition.
Interpret scores, loadings, and reconstructed cells.
Select rank using held out reconstruction.
Test whether VALEX components predict MegaAcceptability profiles.

title: Factorization
text:
Represent the measurements
Rows, columns, origins, and units

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What does one cell of a linguistic data matrix measure?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
For \(\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\),
\[x_{ij}=\text{the value of variable }j\text{ for object }i.\]

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What does \(x_{31}=300\) mean?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Token 3 has an F1 measurement of 300 Hz.
Both indices are required for that interpretation.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
If rows are tokens, scores locate tokens. If rows are speakers, scores locate speakers.
Aggregation changes the represented object.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
Columns define the representation.
Including duration and twice duration gives the same measurement two coordinates.

title: Factorization
text:
Method
Before factorization, record what one row represents, how rows were selected, what each column measures, which columns repeat information, and which collection the objects come from.

title: Factorization
text:
Data
PHOIBLE may contain several inventories for one language from different sources.
The row selection rule must be fixed before a language by segment matrix is interpreted.
PHOIBLE 2.0 documentation

[Sources]
PHOIBLE 2.0 download and citation page: https://phoible.org/download
PHOIBLE FAQ on multiple inventories and sources: https://phoible.org/faq

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What coordinate system should later components use?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Centering changes a column’s origin. Scaling changes its unit.
These operations recall the earlier treatment of centering.

title: Factorization
text:
Method
\[x^c_{ij}=x_{ij}-\bar x_j\]
\[z_{ij}=\frac{x_{ij}-\bar x_j}{s_j}\]

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Durations are 100, 120, and 140 ms.
What are their standardized values?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The mean is 120 ms and the sample standard deviation is 20 ms.
The standardized values are \(-1\), \(0\), and \(1\).

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #3
Giving every column variance one is a weighting decision.
It is not a neutral software default.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #4
New observations must use the training means and standard deviations.
Recomputing them on evaluation observations creates data leakage.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
Factorization reorganizes the information supplied in a matrix. It cannot recover omitted observations or repair a theoretically inappropriate representation.

title: Factorization
text:
Build component patterns
From one outer product to an ordered decomposition

title: Factorization
text:
Question
When can one pattern reproduce every cell of a matrix?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
A nonzero matrix has rank one when it can be written as an outer product:
\[\mathbf X=\mathbf a\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Data
\[
\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}2&4\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}2&4\\4&8\\6&12\end{bmatrix}.
\]

title: Factorization
text:
Interpretation
The first vector varies across rows. The second gives the column pattern.
All rows and columns are proportional.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
Rank is an algebraic property of the matrix.
It is not a psychological construct or a linguistic category.

title: Factorization
text:
Challenge
Most linguistic matrices are not exactly rank one.
We need an ordered set of approximate rank one patterns.

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The singular value decomposition, or SVD, writes
\[\mathbf X=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}.\]

[Sources]
University of Illinois CS 357, Singular Value Decomposition: https://cs357.cs.illinois.edu/textbook/notes/svd.html

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The columns of \(\mathbf U\) are left singular vectors.
The columns of \(\mathbf V\) are right singular vectors.

[Sources]
University of Illinois CS 357, Singular Value Decomposition: https://cs357.cs.illinois.edu/textbook/notes/svd.html

title: Factorization
text:
Output
\[\mathbf X=\sum_{k=1}^r\sigma_k\mathbf u_k\mathbf v_k^{\mathsf T},\qquad \sigma_1\geq\sigma_2\geq\cdots>0.\]
Each term is rank one.

title: Factorization
text:
Interpretation
The singular value \(\sigma_k\) measures the strength of term \(k\) under squared reconstruction error.
The first term is the closest rank one approximation.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
Singular vectors have arbitrary sign.
Replacing \(\mathbf u_k\) and \(\mathbf v_k\) by their negatives leaves the reconstructed matrix unchanged.

[Sources]
Palarea Albaladejo, Principal Components Analysis, sign indeterminacy: https://imae.udg.edu/~jpalarea/StatsDS/principal-components-analysis.html

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #3
Repeated singular values weaken interpretation of individual directions.
The associated subspace is identified more strongly than one orientation within it.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
The SVD orders rank one patterns by their contribution to squared reconstruction of the specified matrix.

title: Factorization
text:
Principal components
Directions of variation around column means

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Which direction through the measured variables has the greatest projected variation?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Principal component analysis, or PCA, finds orthogonal directions in a centered matrix, ordered by projected variance.

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Method
Center the columns, then decompose
\[\mathbf X_c=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma\mathbf V^{\mathsf T}.\]

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The columns of \(\mathbf V\) are the principal component directions.
The score matrix is
\[\mathbf Z=\mathbf X_c\mathbf V=\mathbf U\boldsymbol\Sigma.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Goal
The first direction \(\mathbf v_1\) maximizes
\[\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf X_c\mathbf v)\]
subject to \(\lVert\mathbf v\rVert_2=1\).

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
PCA uses numerical variation in the matrix.
It does not use category labels or a theory of the response unless they were built into the representation.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
If F1 and F2 both increase together across tokens, should the first direction assign them the same sign or opposite signs?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
The same sign represents their common increase.
The complete direction may be multiplied by \(-1\) without changing the component.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
PCA identifies directions that reconstruct centered numerical variation. A direction does not acquire a linguistic interpretation from its rank alone.

title: Factorization
text:
Read and reconstruct components
Row coordinates, variable directions, and residual cells

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Which quantity locates an observation, and which quantity describes a component direction through variables?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Scores locate row observations.
Loadings are the entries of unit length component directions through the original variables.

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Method
For centered row \(\mathbf x_i^c\) and component direction \(\mathbf v_k\),
\[z_{ik}=\mathbf x_i^{c\mathsf T}\mathbf v_k.\]

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
Join scores to linguistic metadata by stable row identifiers.
Row order alone is fragile after filtering or reshaping.

title: Factorization
text:
Interpretation
Read a loading pattern across variables and a score pattern across observations.
Do not interpret one isolated sign without its companion entries and metadata.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
What does retaining the first \(K\) components reproduce?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
A rank-\(K\) approximation is
\[\widehat{\mathbf X}_K=\sum_{k=1}^K\sigma_k\mathbf u_k\mathbf v_k^{\mathsf T}.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Output
The residual matrix is
\[\mathbf E_K=\mathbf X-\widehat{\mathbf X}_K.\]
Every cell records what the retained terms did not reconstruct.

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
For centered data, the proportion of variance explained is
\[\frac{\sum_{k=1}^K\sigma_k^2}{\sum_{k=1}^r\sigma_k^2}.\]

[Sources]
Penn State STAT 508, Lesson 7: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat508/Lesson07.html

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
Observed variance explained is an in sample reconstruction summary.
It is not held out prediction and not a measure of linguistic information.

title: Factorization
text:
Question
How are reconstructed standardized values returned to the original units?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
Multiply each column by its training standard deviation, then add its training mean.
The inverse transformation must use the fitted coordinate system.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
Scores and loadings interpret the low rank coordinates. Reconstruction returns those coordinates to the cells that defined the original linguistic representation.

title: Factorization
text:
Choose the retained rank
Separate fitting, selection, and final evaluation

title: Factorization
text:
Question
How many components should be retained for a declared reconstruction task?

title: Factorization
text:
Approach
Choose the rank that minimizes reconstruction loss on validation cells that did not determine the components.

title: Factorization
text:
Implementation

Fit preprocessing and components on training data.
Evaluate fixed candidate ranks on validation data.
Select one rank using the declared loss.
Refit on training plus validation data.
Evaluate once on untouched test data.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
Centering, scaling, imputation, and component directions are fitted operations.
Each must remain inside the training split.

title: Factorization
text:
Challenge
Observed reconstruction error decreases whenever rank increases.
It therefore cannot choose rank without an external criterion.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #2
A bend in a scree plot describes the singular value sequence.
It does not directly answer which rank predicts held out cells best.

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #3
Cell weighting defines the evaluation target.
Equal cell, row, and variable weighting answer different reconstruction questions.

title: Factorization
text:
Upshot
A selected rank is conditional on the representation, split, candidate set, and loss. It is not the true number of linguistic dimensions.

title: Factorization
text:
Corpus distributions and clause selection
VALEX predictors and MegaAcceptability profiles

title: Factorization
text:
Question
Can a verb’s corpus distribution predict its acceptability across clause embedding frames?

title: Factorization
text:
Answer
A verb’s selectional profile records its acceptability across syntactic frames.
White and Rawlins 2020

[Sources]
White and Rawlins, Frequency, acceptability, and selection: https://doi.org/10.5334/gjgl.1001

title: Factorization
text:
Data
MegaAcceptability supplies 50 frame judgments for each retained verb.
VALEX supplies a 109 dimensional corpus frame distribution for the same verb.
White and Rawlins 2020

[Sources]
White and Rawlins, Frequency, acceptability, and selection: https://doi.org/10.5334/gjgl.1001

title: Factorization
text:
Important Point #1
VALEX counts are converted to within verb proportions.
The predictor represents allocation across complement frames, not total verb frequency.

title: Factorization
text:
Goal
Compare two theoretically distinct predictors for verbs excluded from fitting.
The direct predictor uses all VALEX frame proportions. The factor predictor uses retained PCA scores.

title: Factorization
text:
Method
Both analyses use ridge regression to predict the same 50 response columns.
Only the predictor representation changes.

title: Factorization
text:
Implementation
Outer grouped cross validation excludes complete verbs. Inner validation fits normalization, PCA, rank selection, and the ridge penalty using only the outer training verbs.

title: Factorization
